speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: QUESTIONS AND MOTIONS FOR PRODUCTION OF PAPERS
subsubtopic: HANDLING OF OUT-OF-CONDITION WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a brief statement in regard to the handling of out-of-condition grain arising from the 1951 crop in the prairie provinces. I am making this statement on behalf of my colleague the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) as well as on my own behalf.
As members of the house know, the 1951 grain crop in the west was harvested under very unfavourable circumstances. Of the grain which was harvested last fall, a large proportion was threshed in a tough and damp condition, which has created unprecedented problems for producers themselves, for the Canadian wheat board, the Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada and for grain handling agencies. In addition, according to the dominion bureau of statistics, about 150 million bushels of wheat and 135 million bushels of oats and barley still remain to be threshed.
According to the records of the Canadian wheat board, about 186 million bushels of tough and damp wheat, oats, and barley have now been accepted at country elevators. This compares with 100 million bushels of
tough and damp grain accepted at country elevators in the preceding crop year when the problem of out-of-condition grain was regarded as particularly serious.
Substantial progress has been made in disposing of tough wheat, oats and barley, and about 50 million bushels of tough and damp grain have been dried in terminal elevators at the Pacific coast, in the lake-head and in interior terminal elevators. In addition, damp wheat is being shipped to the United States for drying. However, there are still substantial stocks of tough and damp grain in public storage, and it will be some time before these stocks can be disposed of or dried.
In addition to the quantities of tough and damp grain delivered to the board and the quantities of these deliveries which remain in store, there is a considerable quantity of damp grain which was threshed last fall and still remains on farms. On the basis of recent surveys carried out by the board there were about 36 million bushels of threshed damp wheat on farms in the prairie provinces in mid-February. In addition, there were substantial quantities of threshed tough wheat and threshed tough and damp oats and barley on farms awaiting delivery.
The next sixty to eighty days will be critical from the standpoint of the delivery of present farm stocks of threshed out-ofcondition grain. It is the policy to provide delivery opportunity for these farm stocks of tough and damp grain as soon as physically possible. It will be difficult to complete this task before the warm weather sets in. Producers having tough and damp grain on their farms will have to exercise unusual care in maintaining the condition of these stocks until they can be delivered at country elevators. This, broadly, is the problem which lies ahead in handling threshed out-of-condition grain now on farms.
In view of the circumstances which I have described, I would like to appeal to all producers with unthreshed grain on their farms to use their best efforts to see that their spring threshing does not add to the present problem of out-of-condition grain. Under the circumstances which now prevail, no assurance can be given that there will be a prompt delivery opportunity for grain which is harvested this spring in a tough or damp condition. It should also be emphasized

Grain
that if grain is threshed in the spring with a high moisture content and when the weather is warm, it would be most difficult for handling companies to maintain the condition of this grain in country elevators and while in transit to terminal elevators. This fact should be seriously considered by producers before undertaking the threshing of grain still in the fields in the prairie provinces.
It is apparent that even if spring harvesting is confined to the threshing of dry grain, deliveries of out-of-condition grain for the crop year 1951-52 will total at least 250 million bushels. This is an unprecedented quantity of out-of-condition grain to be received in any crop year, and is taxing and will continue to tax our grain handling facilities to the limit. While a large percentage of the threshed out-of-condition grain has now been delivered at country elevators, substantial farm stocks still remain in certain areas. These areas are now well defined, and the extent of the remaining problem is known. To relieve these areas the best efforts of the Canadian wheat board, the Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada, the transport controller, the handling companies and the railways will be continued.
With the co-operation of all concerned, and especially with the co-operation of producers in respect to their spring threshing, losses arising from the harvesting of so much out-of-condition grain from the 1951 crop can be held at minimum levels. The coming of an early spring will greatly assist in handling the over-all problem of out-of-condition grain, but will make it more difficult for producers to maintain the condition of tough and damp wheat on farms until delivery can be effected.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday last the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked me to report upon the progress in the revision of the statutes. I said then, offhand, that I thought it would take several months, but that I would look into the matter and make a further report, which is as follows:
The statute revision commission was appointed in February, 1949, and immediately after the appointment of the commission a legal and clerical staff was employed by the commission to assist in the consolidation and revision of the statutes. The work has proceeded according to the following successive stages: (1) Preparation of a consolidation from the official texts of the statutes; (2) printing the consolidation; (3) correction of page proofs by clerical staff and revising by the commission of the first print in accordance with the statute revision act; (4) reprinting the revised print; (5) verifying the reprint; and (6) final printing and binding.
In order to complete the whole task as quickly as possible, work on all these stages has proceeded concurrently to the fullest extent that circumstances would permit.
The first three stages are completed and the fourth stage is eighty per cent completed. The fifth stage, namely, verification of the reprint, commenced on the first of March, 1952, and it is expected that the last stage,

namely, final printing and binding, will commence before the end of the current month.
The original consolidation was prepared by a legal staff engaged by the commission, but the work of the revision has been done by the commission itself. Since the work of consolidation is complete, the legal staff of the commission has been reduced to one, who is supervising the printing and is preparing the tables and indexes.
It is expected that the reprinting of the revised prints will be completed this month, that all final text will have been submitted to the queen's printer by the end of April, and that the final printing and binding will be completed towards the end of the current year or early in 1953.
At the last session of parliament the commission was authorized to prepare a supplementary volume to include the statutes enacted at the current session of parliament. The preparation of the supplementary volume will commence at the end of the current session and the supplementary volume will be issued at the same time as the main revision.
In the case of the 1927 revision there were approximately fifty months between the appointment of the commission and the effective date of the revision. It is expected that slightly less time will be required for the new revision, although the material is twenty-five per cent greater, and the task of preparing the consolidation and revision has been complicated somewhat by the fact that during the present revision parliament has been in session for longer periods than was the case in the years immediately preceding the 1927 revision.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called, I wish to ask a question of the Prime Minister. Will the interim report of Mr. Justice Ilsley in regard to war reparations, to which reference was made by the Prime Minister on November 20, 1951, as then being in the hands of the government, be tabled? If so, when may the tabling be expected; and is the Prime Minister yet in a position to say when interim payments can be made to claimants in respect of war losses?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF REPORT-INTERIM PAYMENTS TO CLAIMANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 4 I received the official report of the Right Hon. Mr. Ilsley reporting on the reference that had been made to him in that respect. It is a most comprehensive document, extending over some 166 pages, with certain appendices. At a council meeting today it was received in the usual traditional form for forwarding to His Excellency the Governor General. It was decided at once that the queen's printer would be asked to advise as to what would be the most practical and expeditious manner of getting copies, either by an offset process or by printing, so that they could be made available to those interested.
There are hundreds of recommendations in the form of decisions made by the commissioner in answering questions that had been submitted in the reference, as to what classes of claims should be considered, how they should be filed, how they should be proved, and so on. I am sure that it will be of interest to all prospective claimants as a clear indication of how they will have to proceed to have their claims considered by commissioners and deputy commissioners, and will be of great assistance to the commissioners and deputy commissioners in dealing with these claims.
It was not found practicable to devise rules that could be set up in advance to determine the classes of urgent claims that could be

Inquiries of the Ministry considered, but that is dealt with in the final report. Procedures are suggested in the report to enable these urgent claims to get proper consideration and to be disposed of as expeditiously as possible. There is an indication as to what information should be supplied to those who have indicated that they have what they consider to be urgent claims.
It is intended as soon as that can be done to have the report tabled and to have copies available for those who would have a real interest in securing copies. In view of the very large number of probable claimants, the number of copies available may have to run into the thousands. The offset process gives a good copy. As I say, we want to know if that would be the most practical and expeditious way in which this report may be made available for the information of the public.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), who is indisposed, perhaps I may be permitted to answer this question. In view of the press statements ascribed to Air Vice Marshal T. A. Lawrence, civil defence director for Toronto, about the supply of sirens for the Toronto area, it might be useful for me to make a brief review of the background for the choice of the particular sirens now ready for shipment in quantity to Toronto. Two years ago the selection of a suitable air raid siren for Canada was turned	over to the
defence research board. After the needs of Canadian cities and the characteristics of various models had been thoroughly studied, it was decided early last year that a twin-note siren of the sort used by Great Britain during world war II was still the most satisfactory for all purposes. In reaching this decision, there was the closest collaboration with United Kingdom and United States civil defence authorities, who also were carrying out extensive research in this field.
As a matter of interest, the sirens selected for Canada served effectively in Great Britain during the war years and are now being brought back into use in that country. As sirens of the type decided upon could not be purchased quickly elsewhere, manufacture was arranged in Canada with a company in Toronto.
The decision to select this particular siren was made after satisfactory tests had been carried out in Ottawa and Windsor. The prototype model has also been satisfactorily tested in Winnipeg.
Of the first order placed last year for 200 sirens, 35 were allotted to the Toronto area. After these have been properly sited, it will be possible for the Toronto civil defence authorities to determine their further requirements. The sirens for Toronto have been built in accordance with technical data supplied to Ottawa by the province of Ontario

on May 30 of last year. On February 18 of this year advice was received that the Toronto and York committee on civil defence had just completed a report on sirens. As this report has not yet been received in Ottawa, no amendment has yet been made in instructions given the manufacturer on the basis of the Ontario recommendations of last May.
I might say that Saturday of last week the Minister of National Health and Welfare and General Worthington attended a conference in Toronto with the Ontario minister responsible for civil defence, the mayor of Toronto and the members of the Toronto and York committee on civil defence.
The siren warning system and other important aspects of the civil defence problem were thoroughly reviewed. The co-operative attitude among the three levels of government evident at this meeting will no doubt continue to mark progress in this field.
Full study will of course be given by federal civil defence officers to any further recommendations received on the development of a satisfactory siren warning system for selected Canadian communities. In this connection may I read a telegram which was received from Toronto under date of March 5. It is as follows:

May I again express our appreciation to you for conferring with the Toronto and York civil defence committee last Saturday. speakeroldname: Mr. E. A. McCusker (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PRESS REPORTS WITH RESPECT TO HEALTH EXAMINATION OF IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
I thought this question was effectively answered in the Globe and Mail of March 5, but perhaps it might be wise if I made a short statement with respect to examination of immigrants. This is carried out by forty-three full-time Canadian doctors employed overseas, When emergency requires, additional Canadian doctors who are doing post-graduate work overseas are temporarily employed. X-rays are required of all over the age of II years. Where the parents have given a history or show indications of healed tuberculosis, the children are X-rayed as well.
Physical examination is given and care taken to avoid admitting epileptics, mental oases, tuberculosis, trachoma and venereal disease. I might say that not only is the prospective immigrant examined, but all his family are examined. Then if the head of a family comes to Canada and wants to bring out his family from the old country we know they are physically fit as well. All immigrants must produce a certificate of vaccination at the port of embarkation. The sick are examined at the port of entry and are placed in quarantine in disembarkation hospitals and retained there until they recover. Although the flow of immigration was heaviest in western Canada in the early days of its settlement, the incidence of tuberculosis remained lower in western Canada than in any other part of the country.
Recently Ontario has had a heavy influx of immigrants-104,000 during the past year and* approximately 500,000 since the war. Yet today the incidence of tuberculosis has reached the phenomenal low in Ontario of 13 per 100,000, and the incidence of tuberculosis in immigrants coming to Canada is -043 per cent. The mental cases over the past five years have numbered 200 in 500,000 immigrants, one in 2,500.
When the immigrants arrive in Canada they are given medical care until employed. If immigrants are placed with relatives upon their arrival in Canada they are given no further medical care, but in the case of mass labour immigration they and their dependents are treated locally by medical officers until they are placed' in employment. This medical care is given in co-operation with the Department of Labour and the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. In view of these facts I do not think the criticism is justified.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, March 6, consideration of the motion of Mr. E. W. George for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take very long in this debate. With the exception of the mover (Mr. George) and the seconder (Mr. Gauthier, Lake St. John)-and incidentally I congratulate them most warmly on the very, able speeches they delivered-the speakers, particularly on the opposition side, spent a good deal of time dealing with matters which are perhaps essentially budgetary in their nature. As a preface to the few remarks I am going to make this afternoon it might be useful if I were to announce, subject of course to the usual reservation for unforeseen contingencies, that I intend to bring down my budget on Tuesday, April 8, at the usual hour.
As hon. members will appreciate, this is a time of the year when both I and my officials are kept pretty busy in connection with budgetary preparation. It goes on during the year, but I suppose that in the two or three months that precede the bringing down of the budget I must see literally hundreds of delegations in person and receive a great many more representations in writing from both groups and individual taxpayers; and let me say at once that in my opinion this feature of budget consideration is an essential part of the preparation of the budget. It is true that the government has at its disposal, through official sources and otherwise, complete information with respect to the position of business in general, as well as of individual businesses, but that information can be no substitute for the detailed particulars of the impact of a tax or taxes upon an individual business. For that reason I welcome such data, and I do not see how a fair budget could be prepared unless one were in receipt of assistance of that kind. It enables a finance minister to discharge what after all is his essential duty and responsibility in the preparation of a budget, that is, the distribution of the total burden which has to be imposed upon the taxpayers by as fair a method as it is possible for human ingenuity, wisdom and resourcefulness to devise; and that is what we endeavour to do. That is the sort of representation and assistance I most heartily welcome.
I may say in passing that the treasury board completed its consideration of the estimates last week. They are now in the hands of the printer, and I hope will be tabled in
The Address-Mr. Abbott the house very shortly. So the task from here on is to ascertain what if any changes should be made in our taxation structure, and what form the budget should take.
There is, however, something which has arisen more particularly within the course of the last two or three years which has given me a good deal of concern, and which I did not experience earlier in my tenure of office as Minister of Finance. That is a form of activity by special pressure groups, I suppose referred to as lobbies, a type of activity which I think has been considerably more common in other countries, and perhaps more particularly in the United States, where the governmental system is different from our own. What prompted me to make the remarks I am making now was a circular letter which came to my attention only yesterday morning. I am going to ask the house to bear with me while I read it in full, because I think, or at least I hope, the house will agree that in certain of its aspects this circular letter is an insult to the intelligence of the members of the house and a reflection upon their integrity.
The letter to which I refer was sent out by the federation of automobile dealer associations of Canada. Let me hasten to say that I have a great many friends among automobile dealers. Indeed one of my oldest friends is a very successful automobile dealer, and I do not for a moment think that most of the dealers who may belong to this association would be sympathetic to the sort of material put out in this circular letter. This is on the letterhead of the federation of automobile dealer associations of Canada, with executive offices at 145 Yonge street, Toronto 1, Ontario, and is dated December 27, 1951.
It reads-and many of the words (see italics) are underlined:
Bulletin No. 166
To Members of Member Associations:
Federation is now in the midst of an intensified campaign to persuade the government to ease present discriminatory credit restrictions and taxes. We need your help-we must have it-to impress upon the public and the government that a national protest against such discrimination is developing.
Let me interject that I have no quarrel with a statement of that kind.
As one major step in this campaign, we urge you to talk to your local member of parliament NOW, during the parliamentary recess, about this problem that so vitally affects you and the people as a whole. Talk to him through your association. If you can't do that, talk to him individually-the main thing is to see him right away, regardless of his party affiliation.
I have no quarrel with the circular up to that point.
We have retained Editorial Services Limited, of Toronto, Montreal and Ottawa, as public relations

The Address-Mr. Abbott
counsel to advise and help federation in this campaign. Your interview with your M.P. is an essential part of our plan.
Members of parliament understand, appreciate and value good publicity. We want you to enlist your member as a spokesman for our cause, and, when you do, we through Editorial Services, will provide a great deal of national publicity for him- publicity he will like and that will do you a lot of good.
This is how we will create that publicity:
1.	Induce your M.P. to authorize statements which can be used by Editorial Services for publicity on a national basis.
2.	We likely will be able to arrange (through an established speakers' bureau) for the member to address an important club or other public body on the subject. There will be similar nation-wide publicity on his speech.
3.	It may be possible for Editorial Services to get your member on the air, for a talk, forum, or interview. The same coast to coast publicity will follow.
4.	When he speaks about our troubles in the house, a report of his speech will go to all wire services, every newspaper and every radio station in Canada, through Editorial Services' plan.
Your job will be to advise us of the member's intentions. Editorial Services will get in touch with him immediately in order to publicize his statement in every possible way.
The men who plan the budget and who will modify or continue the present discrimination against our industry, and the public, will heed the pressure of public opinion as expressed through national publicity. That is why we emphasize the importance of stressing publicity value to your member.
Here is What We Urge You to Do
1.	Arrange an early interview with your M.P.- right now, while he is at home. Parliament will reassemble about the middle of January-you must talk to him immediately.
2.	Know the subject thoroughly before you see him. Here are the key points to stress:
(a)	Both credit restrictions and taxation are discriminatory-they impose an unjust burden upon people who must have cars for work or business, and upon an essential industry.
(b)	They are a genuine hardship on average and low wage earners.
(c)	They are a special hardship upon manual workers. If you wish, read to your member all or part of D. A. Amory's brief that begins on page 38 of the report of the 1951 F.A.D.A. annual meeting.
Be sure you read and understand the digest of facts enclosed, then leave it with your member.
3.	Don't bore or confuse your member with a lot of figures and statistics during the interview. The digest you hand him can speak for you.
4.	You probably have a most potent weapon in the experience of your own business-better than the general facts, which do not always impress a member. He has the interests of his own constituents closest at heart.
Make your interview a "home-town deal"\
(a)	If you are suffering because of credit terras, tell your member-tell him how much.
(b)	It would be well, if you are in trouble, to tell him how much. He is interested in you, as well as every other voter.
(c)	Point out the number of people in your community-in his constituency-who must have automobiles in order to make a living.

(d)	If you know of any actual examples of hardship because would-be purchasers can't afford essential automobiles as a result of present credit terms or "luxury" taxes (or both), tell your M.P.
5.	We want first to have credit restrictions relaxed. It is generally believed that big monthly payments are the greatest obstacle to prospective purchasers.
6.	Don't forget to emphasize how the public suffers through discrimination.
There are many more people than dealers, and, although your M.P. will be interested in your plight, he will be more interested in the plight of the people affected by unfair credit terms and taxes.
7.	Finally, ask your member to act:
(a)	To speak out at Ottawa, and anywhere else where it may do good, on your behalf, and on behalf of credit-hit and tax-hurt would-be purchasers-the public as a whole. He will want the resulting publicity-and so do we!
(b)	To urge the Minister of Finance to amend the credit regulations (primarily) as you believe they should be changed.
(c)	To promise that he will seek relief for you and the public immediately upon his return to Ottawa, and that he will write you the result of his efforts, for your own information and for publicity.
8.	Inform federation quickly of your efforts and results, so that we and our public relations counsel may take advantage of every opportunity for publicity.
9.	We haven't much time-arrange your interview today-the quicker we and you can influence public opinion, the quicker we will get relief.
10.	Please return the report on the enclosed form promptly.
With best wishes for success in this project, and our heartiest thanks for your co-operation,
Howard B. Moore General Manager
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am not going to comment on that letter. I think it speaks for itself. May I say to the house, and I am sure this view is shared by all hon. members, that the finance minister is particularly allergic to both pressure and pressure groups. As I said earlier in my remarks, I welcome, I invite representations by individual taxpayers or groups of taxpayers. I strongly object to these tactics, which I am afraid have been common in other jurisdictions but in my experience have not been known here until recently, and which attempt indirectly to influence members of parliament.
That is my first point, and the second is related to it. It is related to tobacco and the tax on tobacco. There has been a great deal of talk about the tax being too high, and I have not the slightest quarrel with that talk or with that argument. The tobacco growers have seen me on two occasions, and have provided me with an extremely well prepared and very helpful brief which has been carefully considered. I have had representations from the tobacco companies and from others indicating that they thought the

tax was too high and ought to be reduced. Those were the usual representations the Minister of Finance receives, and I have no quarrel with those representations.
However, I have also a file of letters from retail dealers informing me that they have had great difficulty in obtaining adequate supplies of cigarettes over the past few months. I should say that most of those letters are prefaced with the statement: We want you to have this information hut we do not want to get in wrong with the tobacco companies, so we would like you to treat this letter as confidential. Of course, I have done so. There are some which are not in that category, and one of the most recent is one I hold in my hand. It is dated February 28, 1952, and is from Mr. Slaven, a druggist in Sydney, Nova Scotia. It reads:
Hon. D. C. Abbott, Q.C., M.P.
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir:
I was certainly pleased to notice by the press that you were aware what the tobacco companies were doing.
While we hated to lose sales, it annoyed us to realize the tobacco companies were trying to mislead the government and the public.
As a matter of interest, and also to substantiate your statements:
Shortly after the settlement of their strike at Montreal their agent (Imperial Tobacco Company) came in and cut our stock, taking back anything that was over a month old (the normal amount on hand is two months supply). They did that with the retailers the first month; the following month they did it with the wholesalers; they tried to kid us it was done on purpose so that we would always have very fresh stock on hand.
After doing that we found our orders were cut to about one quarter of our needs. Until you made that statement at the end of the year that no change would be made, they kept reducing the orders, the result being that we would have Imperial cigarettes for three days and then have none on our shelves for four or five days.

Based on the increased price our dollar sales volume would have been much greater than the previous period.
I'm a non-smoker but I believe the tax is too high. However I do object to the method used by the company in an attempt to intimidate you and force your hand.
Yours sincerely,
George B. Slaven
Mr. Slaven is a man after my own heart.

I should like first to compliment the mover (Mr. George) and the seconder (Mr. Gauthier, Lake St. John) of the address. Their speeches were well prepared, interesting and well delivered. The debate on the address affords me an opportunity of discussing the situation confronting the textile industry, which is of marked importance to the constituency of Lanark and the whole Dominion of Canada.
Lanark has twelve textile mills, and the recession in that industry has been responsible for considerable unemployment, particularly in the latter part of 1951. It reached its peak in the first month of this year. The plants in this area are chiefly in the wool textile and knitting branches.
208	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Blair Government orders for textile products have been of considerable assistance in easing out a difficult situation. In fact, some of these mills would be shut down if it were not for defence contracts. Defence contracts for 26 million yards of fabric and
750.000	blankets have avoided more serious trouble. Many plants are on short time or have dropped second shifts. Some have reduced first shifts to the point where there is a lay-off of from five to forty per cent of the workers.
In obtaining these highly competitive contracts, plants had to cut their prices down to costs in order to keep running. However, defence contracts are temporary business and industry will require something more in order to be maintained. But before entering into a discussion of the present conditions existing in the industry, it would be well to place before the house a review of the importance of the textile industry as manufacturers of textile products, and also so far as manufacturing is concerned. The industry has 791 plants in Canada and employs over
100.000	men and women. Plants exist in 269 communities in Canada. I submit a table showing the number of plants, municipalities and the number of employees by provinces.

It will be noted that while the major number of plants are located in Ontario and Quebec, the industry is growing in western Canada and gives employment to almost
4,000	people in the maritimes and Newfoundland. It ranks first in Canada in wages and salaries paid. It is interesting by way of comparison to note that the gross annual production of the industry is over $700 million. This is equal to five times the amount of Canada's gold production, and is more than the combined value of the wheat and the oat crop of Canada. It is mainly an industry of small towns and villages, and in many cases comprises the main source of employment. One-third of the 791 factories are located in towns and villages with a population of fewer than 5,000 people, and half the mills are in communities of fewer than 25,000 people. In some of the towns in the Ottawa valley 100 per cent of all the persons who are engaged in manufacturing are textile workers. In the larger centres, 

there are as many people engaged in primary textile mills as in all other manufacturing establishments combined.
Textile mills in the Ottawa valley in one year, 1949, paid out over $3 million in salaries and wages, and they spent $4,750,000 for raw materials. Workers in textile mills in Canada are among the highest paid textile workers in the world. Since 1939 there has been an upward revision of wages and the wage rate is now 280 per cent of the rate on that date. In common with all wage earners the present high cost of living is becoming a serious problem. The average or late earnings of primary textile workers in Great Britain are about 45 per cent of the earnings of Canadian textile workers, France 35 per cent, Italy 34 per cent, Czechoslovakia 33 per cent, The Netherlands 32 per cent, Germany 27 per cent and Japan 7 per cent. The average earnings of primary textile workers in Canada is not quite as high as in the United States, but the same differential exists when similar industries in Canada and in the United States are compared. The tariff on textiles entering the United States bears a higher ratio to Canadian tariffs than United States textile wages bear to Canadian wages.
The woollen and knit goods branch of the industry provides employment for 42,500 people. It is comprised of 567 mills located in 170 localities. These mills produce principally blankets, carpets, worsted cloth and knitted goods. The industry is expanding and since 1945 it has spent $250 million on new equipment and expansion. It becomes apparent therefore that the textile industry is a very important branch of our Canadian economy.
In a period of war or preparation for war a healthy textile industry becomes as important in the production of material as those industries producing guns or aeroplanes. Since 1939, the textile industry of Canada has been capable of meeting the demands for war materials and at the same time has been able to meet the civilian requirements for goods. The large number of employees form an important market for Canadian farm products.
In the war of 1939-1945 practically all the textiles used by the Canadian forces were made out of Canadian materials. We can well be proud of the record of this industry. In that period Britain and the United States could not have supplied Canada's requirements, and in fact the Canadian industry was called upon to supply quantities of materials to our allies in addition to supplying our own civilian and war demands.

During the past six months the industry has suffered a recession. Imports from Britain, United States, Italy and other European countries, have offered severe competition to our Canadian mills. Our tariff is lower than that of any other country in the world in so far as textiles are concerned, except Sweden, and in that country all imports are controlled. A great percentage of the wool fabrics that have been imported into Canada came from Great Britain, and there is no control or restriction on the volume of those imports. The following list gives the average duty charged by countries on the f.o.b. price of the four standard types of woollen cloth: Australia, 32 per cent; Belgium, 31 per cent; Canada, 13-1 per cent; France, 33-9 per cent; Germany, 23-7 per cent; Great Britain, 20-8 per cent; Italy, 27 per cent; The Netherlands, 18-9 per cent; Spain, 126-6 per cent; Sweden, 5-6 per cent; United States, 36 [DOT] 4 per cent.
The woollen and worsted cloth branch of the industry has been mainly affected by imports. In 1949 the woollen mills of Canada supplied 63 per cent of the domestic market, but by 1951 this had fallen to 53 per cent, and some 2,500 workers were unemployed. In worsted fabrics, the Canadian mills dropped from 47 per cent of the domestic market to 39 per cent in 1951. Britain ranks as the chief exporter of woollen goods to Canada, and has now obtained an increasing share of our domestic market, amounting to 86 per cent of all imports. Canadian wages are double the British rates -and this added to a low 13| per cent tariff on United Kingdom woollens makes it very difficult for our mills to meet the competition. Other low wage countries have increased their sales accordingly.
A recent report of the bureau of statistics shows that the import of fibres and textiles increased to $483.5 million for the year 1951 as against $364.5 million the year previous.
The record of wool fabric imports for the past 12 years is interesting. Pre-war and wartime figures are not too significant. When an industry has invested money, built plants and employed people, it cannot appreciate being driven back to some prior point in history.

It is not sufficient to state that Canada is a mature industrial nation. It is true that, with better equipped factories, we can now stand competition. But the situation as regards the importation of textiles is much more complicated, especially British competition. We must make it possible for the British to earn money here in order to buy our primary products. We are sympathetic to a program of helping Britain, and to help the British nation reestablish itself as a great world power. In the cause of peace and for the security of the world Britain must be strong.
However, we must give consideration to the fact that Britain and other European countries have lower manufacturing costs for textiles than in Canada because of the lower labour costs, and some degree of subsidization. The volume of textile importations is now replacing Canadian-made materials. It does not seem fair that the textile industry should bear the whole brunt of imports to the point of unemployment.
Speaking in the budget debate on Novem-1951 ber 1, 1949, as reported in Hansard at page 2U4	1360, I made this statement-and remember,

210	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Blair
national interest for the textile industry to be forced to close its doors, and for workers, who have given many years of their lives to developing this trade, to be thrown out on the street to look for work wherever they can find it. Unless external conditions and factors today threatening this vitally important industry are closely studied, and their effect constantly observed by the government, the conditions I have just warned about are not beyond the realm of possibility.
Earlier in the same speech I said:
This industry played a most important part in the war effort of Canada, and in my opinion it is essential that it be maintained as a healthy, virile industry as part of our economic defence plans of the future.
Imports of cotton goods are increasing. At one time previous to 1939, our mills supplied 70 per cent of all our domestic requirements. Last year this had been reduced to 58 per cent. In 1950, the United States exported 147 million yards to Canada, and last year increased their exports to this country by over 10 million yards. Low wage countries such as Japan, Holland, and Czechoslovakia increased their cotton exports to Canada by 100 per cent.
The amount of full-fashioned hosiery from the United States has increased. Such goods may be sold at a loss in Canada by American manufacturers, provided they sell for the same price in the United States. This is one means of unloading surplus stock.
The United States has increased her exports to Canada of synthetic textile dresses for women. In 1949 we imported 114,228 garments, in 1950 we imported 186,502 garments or dresses. The Canadian import quotas on garments were removed early in 1951. Canadian synthetic textile manufacturers feel that American manufacturers are using the Canadian market to unload surpluses. This branch of the industry employs over 20,000 people.
Japan has invaded the field of knitted goods. Last year 30 per cent of the sales on the Canadian glove market were Japanese gloves. Japan pays textile workers one-twelfth of the Canadian wage rate.
The Canadian textile industry is entirely dependent on the Canadian market. Canadian exports in textiles are very small for the reason that Canadian costs of production make it impossible for Canadian goods to compete on outside markets. The products of the Canadian industry are varied. Every piece of imported textiles is competitive with our products. This is shown in the statistics of yardage. In 1949 our wool cloth mills supplied 64 per cent of Canadian consumption, and today only supply 54 per cent. The knitting branch of the industry has now lost 20 per cent of the market.
IMr. Blair.]

We must be prepared to accept imports to pay for our exports. It would not be possible to arrive at a stage where all imports are not competitive. But there is no reason why we cannot arrange standards of competition. We do not want to arrive at a situation where we will give up part of the British market to other countries who will take their goods in payment. The Canadian industry imports a large amount of yarns and wool. It should be possible to devise a policy that would encourage the Canadian industry and at the same time not deprive the British. In order to develop trade channels between Britain and Canada neither country can risk taking unfair advantage in working out trading agreements.
Canadian textile workers have been affected in larger proportions than before, and, as Canadian wages are among the highest paid for this work and Canadian customs duties are quite low in comparison with those of other countries, these differences have caused unemployment. Canadian unions have sent delegations to Ottawa to intercede with the government. Some long-range program is required. If this is not devised, our mills will have no defence against imports which are produced more cheaply in other countries.
There are factors other than competition which have helped create the present slump in textiles. At the outbreak of the Korean war there was a very sharp rise in prices. Buyers overbought because they thought there would be a period when cloth would be in short supply. The price of raw materials increased tremendously and they were difficult to obtain. While it was thought that the buying boom which had started at the outbreak of the Korean war would be temporary, it was not anticipated that the market would break so quickly.
The Canadian consumer is interested in the cost of commodities and these are often reflected in the cost of the raw materials. The price of wool increased 300 per cent last season and in a short time was down to the level of the previous year. Again, in the fall of 1951, it suddenly jumped 60 per cent in one week. Clothing prices to the consumer do not react accordingly and the price of wool in the spring of 1951 was never reflected in the retail price for wool textiles. It must be remembered that there is a period of approximately 15 months before wool reaches the retailer in the form of manufactured goods. This allows for the averaging of costs.
In the period to which I have referred, that of the Korean war, it took six to ten times the amount of capital to finance inventories. About this time credit restrictions were

applied. Customers could not accept orders and when buying was slowed down the mills were left with heavy inventories. Bank or credit restrictions, applying principally to one hundred per cent Canadian-owned companies, further cramped the financial ability to provide working capital and to meet reinvestment in inventories. The clamping down of credit restrictions coincided with the peak of the raw material markets. This financial problem was further complicated by having to meet substantial increases in wage rates, higher taxes and so on.
Substantial increases in the price of food, housing, rental and the cost of living in general have resulted in the public not being able to buy at these high prices. The shrinking world demand for textiles, necessitating the liquidation of inventories, is a common problem to the textile industry throughout the world. It is true of the Canadian textile industry as well. Canada is not a large exporter of textiles and this industry is almost wholly dependent upon the domestic market. Today, because of the almost universal effort to liquidate inventories, European and United States manufacturers are quoting prices in Canada that make it impossible for a domestic manufacturer to compete, except in a few specialties which require prompt delivery. Today imports from Italy are replacing British as well as Canadian cloth, as our mills go on short time with some being actually shut down, two of which are in my own constituency.
The question in the minds of many Canadians is whether or not dumping is responsible for the situation which has arisen and, if so, to what extent? Some months ago a joint labour-management committee of the textile and needle trades protested to the Canadian government against the dumping of United States goods in the Canadian market at prices with which it was impossible to compete and stated that such action was causing widespread unemployment in the industry.
At that time the press reported that the assistant deputy minister of customs assured the delegation that departmental experts had worked out a course which they believed would remedy the situation. This report implies, if it implies anything, that the government recognizes that dumping actually exists and that they have worked out a solution. So far as I have heard, there has been no action by the government to meet this situation. Meanwhile Canadian mills are continuing to slow down or have discontinued operations. An example of this is the recent
The Address-Mr. Fair closing down of a part of the Courtaulds plant at Cornwall for an indefinite period.
Parliament should be informed now if dumping is actually taking place and, if so, what action the government proposes to take under existing statutes for the prevention of such practices. Unemployment in the industry is increasing and would be more serious were it not for the temporary palliative of defence orders which make it possible for mills to continue operations, if only on a part-time basis. But defence orders are not permanent. This whole problem must be considered in the light of present-day competition. The textile industry of Canada is an essential part of our economy. Should the present cold war materialize into an allout conflict, this industry will be called upon to play its part as it did in the last war. It must not be allowed to pass out of existence because our government has failed to take the action which is necessary and which is within its power under existing statutes.

Mr. Speaker, as is customary in this debate, my first word is one of congratulation to the mover (Mr. George) and the seconder (Mr. Gauthier, Lake St. John) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne on the excellent job they did in their statements.
I realize, as do many others, that at the present time our country is faced with many difficulties, not the least of which is the recent outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in and around Regina. I was glad to see that on Wednesday evening we succeeded in passing Bill No. 7, for the control and extirpation of foot-and-mouth disease.
It took some considerable time to pass that bill as a number of angles were discussed and considerable information disseminated. It is now our hope that no further time will be lost in doing everything necessary to stamp out this disease. During the first three days of the week there was considerable discussion about the officials of the department and the veterinary surgeons who were concerned with this disease. It is not my intention at this time in any way to condemn or criticize these officials. These men are not here to speak for themselves. They will be before the agriculture committee a little later and it will be time enough for us to judge their efficiency or otherwise after we have heard from them.
I repeat my request to the government to make the compensation quite generous to men who have lost stock. By doing that they will encourage farmers whose stock may be affected later on to make an early report of any outbreak that may occur.

The Address-Mr. Fair
There is another matter that I want to take up in that connection. I hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), and their colleagues will give favourable consideration to exempting from income tax assessments any amounts that may be paid by way of compensation to those farmers. I feel that is only fair and right because they are losing considerable money and also the opportunity to make money during the time that their farms are denuded of livestock. Again, they will be using the money they are now paid as compensation to purchase livestock to restock their farms later on. I feel that irreparable damage has been done by the prolonged debate that took place in the house. It would have been much better if the bill had been passed in much less time because the publicity that has now spread all over Canada, the United States and other places will not do us any good. Action was needed at that time, and I hope we will have action now without any further delay.
In the speech from the throne there is the following:
You will be asked to consider legislation to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1946, and the Veterans Benefit Act, 1951.
I am very glad to see that announcement in the speech from the throne because for many months we have been pressing the government to make better allowances available to burnt-out pensioners. As a basis for the claim of these people I should like to read into the record once again the promise made by Sir Robert Borden when addressing the Canadian fighting forces at Vimy Ridge in 1917. In part it is as follows:
You are men actually facing the enemy day and night. You are suffering greatly from fatigue, overstrain and lack of rest. The marvel of it is that men could undergo such strain without breaking; but you have never yet broken, and history will appreciate that in days to come ... I give you this assurance: that you need have no fear that the government and the country will fail to show just appreciation of your service to the country and empire in what you are about to do and what you have already done . . . The government and the country will consider it their first duty to see that a proper appreciation of your effort and of your courage is brought to the notice of the people at home, and it will always be our endeavour to so guide the attitude of public opinion that the country will support the government to prove to the returned man its just and due appreciation of the inestimable value of the services rendered to the country and empire; and that no man, whether he goes back or whether he remains in Flanders, will have just cause to reproach the government for having broken with the men who won and the men who died.
This is the promise that was made by the then prime minister of Canada. Though it was made some thirty-five years ago, I feel

it is just as binding on the government of today and the people of Canada today as it was at that time. On the 17th of May last the Canadian Legion presented a brief to the special committee which was sitting at that time to deal with veterans affairs. They asked for certain improvements in the benefits payable to burnt-out pensioners, disability pensioners and others. While at the last session the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) did bring in legislation which was quite satisfactory as far as the disability pensioners are concerned, nothing whatever was done for the burnt-out pensioners, but he did make the statement that early in this session the special committee on veterans affairs would be set up again and that any recommendation made by that committee could be made retroactive to the first of January this year.
Because practically everybody in the country has been receiving pay increases and because the value of our dollar has now decreased to about 50 cents, I feel that the burnt-out pensioners also deserve to have an increase. Many of them are not able to work. Many of them have suffered plenty up to the present time, and I believe it is now our duty to increase their allowances at least to the same extent as we did those of the disability pensioners. Therefore I hope no time will be lost in looking after this matter.
I understand that in the province of Alberta legislation is being proposed to provide pensions for needy widows 60 to 65 years of age if it can be proved that they are in need of such pension. While we have granted old age pensions to an increased number, I feel that the amount of such pensions should be further increased. There does not seem to be very much done to bring down the cost of living, and because of the decrease in the value of the dollar I feel that a further increase of at least $10 a month for old age pensioners would be very welcome and would help to keep them out of financial difficulties.
There is another group for whom many of us have advocated help for some time. I refer to the physically incapacitated, and I am not speaking of those who are 60 years of age and over. I refer to all those who are physically incapacitated and are not able to earn their own living. Many people in Canada, with full use of all their limbs and senses, are having a great deal of difficulty in making a living, and one can realize how much harder it is for those who are physically incapacitated. For the past two years I believe the provincial governments have been making a survey to secure information about these people, and as soon as the results of the survey are made known I hope that no

time will be lost in doing something for them. I hope that before the end of the session the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) will introduce legislation to provide pensions for them.
Another matter that has caused quite a little talk for some time is the trans-Canada highway. In the press not many months ago I read an article to the effect that there is still some difficulty about the Kicking Horse pass route. If some of us had had our way earlier in the program the trans-Canada highway route would not have gone that way. We pointed out on many occasions that bad snow conditions exist there in the winter and sometimes in the summer as well. There was a good illustration of that only last summer, and I understand they are now having difficulties about the route through the Kicking Horse pass. The government of Alberta was blamed for being responsible for approving that route, but I think they were wrongly blamed. The provinces of Saskatchewan and British Columbia favoured the southern route, and it would seem to be foolishness for the government of Alberta to do anything but approve and build the connecting link.
It will give service to at least the southern part of Alberta which is not nearly as heavily populated as central and northern Alberta. However, Alberta will not be content with that, and it is the intention of their government to have no less than three highways spanning the province from east to west. By the end of this summer it is the intention to have highway No. 16 from Lloydminster to Edmonton completed. Most of it is paved at the present time. Approximately 46 or 47 miles still remain to be paved, and the program of the government provides for the completion of that work during the coming summer. In the Edmonton Journal of February 8, under the heading "British Columbia officials studying Yellowhead road", we find this:
A new British Columbia transprovincial highway from the Alberta boundary through the Yellow-head pass to take in the existing road system leading from Kamloops to the Pacific coast, is being studied, according to a report from Victoria.
Public works department planners and officials of Trans-Mountain Oil Pipeline Company, which will start shortly on the construction of an oil pipeline from Edmonton by way of Jasper to Vancouver, are meeting in Victoria. They are trying to co-ordinate necessary road planning particularly in the North Thompson valley.
Public works officials in Victoria have stated that a new transprovincial highway to include the North Thompson highway is "bound to come", paralleling the pipeline route.
I believe we were on sound ground two or three years ago when we advocated the Yellowhead pass route and that we are on sound ground today, and that in the near
The Address-Mr. Fair future we will have a hard surfaced highway through the most practical and appropriate route across the Rockies-the Yellowhead pass.
Now I go to another subject with which I am quite familiar, having been very close to it for the past thirty-eight years. For a little while I should like to discuss the question of agriculture. In the Rural Cooperator of February 26 last, published in Toronto, under the heading "Farmers take the rap" we find this editorial:
Everything indicates that the Canadian farmer is about to take a beating. In fact, he has already begun to have a taste of it.
Prices are falling. Eggs. Poultry. Beef. Hogs. Lamb. They are all on the toboggan.
The farmer isn't feeling very happy about it. If other groups in the country were also taking a licking it mightn't make him any happier, but at least he wouldn't have the feeling that it is all so very unjust and unfair.
Industrial workers in Canada are still getting pay increases. They haven't lost a strike in years. When their living costs go up they ask for more money and with or without a strike they usually end up getting more money.
The^investor class seems to get its increases without even asking for them. Corporate profits last year increased nearly 25 per cent over the previous year.
But the farmers' income is shrinking.
Why?
Perhaps one of the reasons may be that the Canadian government is not at this time particularly interested in seeing farm prices maintained.
There is reason to believe, on the contrary, that the government is privately gratified that farm prices are on the skids.
We have heard on excellent authority that certain economists at Ottawa have advanced the opinion that the most convenient-and politically safe-way to check inflation in this country is to depress farm prices.
Just as an aside, they are doing a very good job of it.
Our government may have listened to that advice.
Our government could also check inflation by freezing wages and corporation profits.
But that would take an extraordinary amount of political courage. Organized labour is powerful and controls a lot of votes. Big business, too, is said to have at least a moderate influence on parliament hill.
So it looks as if the farmer is going to be the scapegoat in Ottawa's crusade against inflation.
There is more to the editorial but I will not quote it further. Let me say in the first place that we have no more loyal group in Canada than our farmers, and that applies to farmers all across the country, in every province. Anyone who doubts that has only to look at their record of performance during the two world wars. Then if we want to find out how they have been treated all we have to do is go back to the beginning of 1946, and see how they were dealt with by the income tax department. The production necessary for the war was all finished. Old

The Address-Mr. Fair men and men unfit for military service worked many more hours than they should have worked, with no knowledge that they would be compelled to pay income tax, and no idea that they would be required to account to the income tax department. In January, 1946, however, immediately after the Christmas holidays, farmers were notified to attend at certain points and give an accounting of their business as far back as 1941. That has been a rather unhappy experience for many of the farmers on the prairies, and in one form or another that investigation is continuing. Many farmers feel they are not being trusted by the Department of National Revenue. On June 29 last the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) had this to say at page 4903 of Hansard:
After all. while we are not members on the government side of the house, we are often expected to give answers to questions dealing with government administration. I agree with the hon. member for Lake Centre that it seems that in Saskatchewan there is more activity in this regard than anywhere else in the dominion.

One of the reasons for that is that there appears to be a little more difficulty in getting the necessary information in Saskatchewan.
In my opinion that statement questions the honesty of the farmers of that province; and since in my own province, and Manitoba, we have a similar number of investigators out through the country, exactly the same cloud is cast upon the farmers of those provinces, and I do not like it. I have made that quite clear to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue on many occasions previously, and when the budget debate is under way we hope to have something more to say about it. The administration of the Income Tax Act as far as farmers are concerned has been discussed on many occasions, but many questions still remain unanswered. We hope that during the budget debate or on the national revenue estimates the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) will answer some of our questions in connection with that administration.
An example of the treatment given the farmers was the wheat agreement between the Canadian government and the British government. If we compare the prices received under that agreement with the prices paid for class II wheat sold by the wheat board to countries other than Britain, we find that the farmers had a loss of $367 million; after they had been given a token payment of $65 million as government conscience money. During that same period of 1946 to 1949, both years inclusive, because the Canadian government decided to be generous with the farmers' money and supply wheat to Canadian millers for consumption in Canada by poor and rich

alike, the 232,000 wheat growers of the prairie provinces lost an additional $137 million.
Then the international wheat agreement came along, the first of its kind. I believe a mistake was made which should not have been made, and I mention this now so that when the agreement is renegotiated some time during the coming summer that pitfall will be avoided, which at the present time is costing the farmers approximately 55 cents a bushel. That is too much of a handout to take away from the farmers while they are suffering from other injustices. Maximum and floor prices are provided under the agreement for each of the years it covers, but the pitfall in the agreement was pointed out by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch). No attention was paid to him, and as a result the farmers have lost millions of dollars. That loss is continuing. The same may be said of the policy of supplying wheat to Canadian millers for home consumption at the price fixed by the international wheat agreement. Again that is not good enough. Why should 232,000 wheat growers in the prairie provinces subsidize Canadians from one ocean to the other to the extent of 55 cents a bushel, so they may be able to eat cheap bread? In the United States they have a program of parity prices for agricultural products. For a number of years many of us on this side of the house have advocated that a similar program be put into effect here. Only last fall, however, when we were discussing the Agricultural Products Act, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) refused to have the Agricultural Prices Support Act amended by inserting a formula which would provide parity prices for the various agricultural products. We have been told by many that this country should produce more food. At Montreal, when speaking to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) spoke along that line. I am not going to read the whole of the newspaper report in that connection, but again it is taken from the Edmonton Journal of January 23. The article reads in part as follows:
Stressing the need for increased productivity on Canadian farms, he told the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in an address prepared for delivery to its annual meeting:
"The population of the whole world is growing very fast, and apart altogether from political rivalries, I doubt if we can ever hope for the secure peace in the world which we all want so much as long as great numbers of people are barely able to eke out an existence bordering on, or in many cases below, the subsistence level."
Happily, Canada was able to look after her own needs and provide a great deal of food for export.
"But those in the world who are not so fortunate as we in this North American continent are becoming more and more aware of their poverty in relation to our plenty-

"We can improve still further our farming methods and go on increasing our productivity and thus meet our own needs and do our share to meet that world problem."
You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister did not tell us anything about the prices that would be obtained for those products. Our experience has been that just as soon as there is a surplus the price of farm products drops and the farmer takes the whole rap.
In the Ottawa Journal of March 6, under the heading "Countries with abundance must share with less fortunate, says CARE director," there appears a statement made by the acting director to the cooperative union at the Chateau Laurier a few days ago. This official also points out the need for increased production.
Then we have Mr. Hannam, the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, speaking to the same body and I shall read one paragraph from this speech:
There can be no peaceful living for us here until we help other countries come up to our own standards. The peoples of Asia want food, land, and human dignity.
Much more could be said, but I am reading these statements simply to point out that the officials of worth-while organizations are indicating the need for greater food production. It might be noted here that when Mr. Hannam was speaking at the Canadian Federation of Agriculture convention in Montreal he did not advocate increased production.
There is an article in the Western Producer of January 31,	1952, under the heading
"C.F.A. delegates uneasy about markets and prices for food; conclude session." It reads:
Representatives of organized farm groups in nine of Canada's ten provinces kept an uneasy eye fixed on the international trade situation throughout all of their discussions at the 16th annual convention of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in Montreal last week.
Delegates were frankly uneasy at the prospect. They pointed out on more than one occasion during their public sessions that international and national leaders were urging them to produce more food for a hungry world, but nobody told them how they were going to sell it or what they might receive for it.
The best authority on agricultural subjects in Canada of whom I know is the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). While the minister has been condemned in many parts of this country, I want to say here that had he had a little help in the cabinet instead of so much opposition we would have had a better and sounder program for agriculture. The minister understands the business. He understands also that unless we have a prosperous agriculture we cannot have a prosperous Canada. This is what the
The Address-Mr. Fair minister had to say in reply to some questions put to him after he had made his speech to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in Montreal. The article is headed, "Gardiner's views." It reads:
Agriculture Minister Gardiner, in a hard-headed, practical approach, told delegates he was making no production suggestions. He outlined the facts as he saw them: how farmers acted on them was up to the farmers themselves. Farmers today were prosperous. The government was prepared to protect them against disastrous losses in the event of a drastic market down-turn. It was not prepared to offer incentive prices for greater production. Farmers knew what marketing prospects were and should govern themselves accordingly.
I think that is one of the greatest condemnations of any government that could be uttered. We have a great country today, but not very much is being done to take care of our surpluses. At the FAO meeting in Rome not long ago the minister is quoted as having said that Canada could increase production but doubted if she would, because no market outlet was assured. It would appear from the statement I quoted that the minister has not *changed his mind. I am not sure whether any plans are being undertaken by the government to get rid of our surplus products, but I feel that something must be done. One of the best methods of helping the farmer would be to cut the cost of production.
I should like to say a word about farm implements. Anything I may say in this connection will not bring any condemnation upon implement agents, because today, while the price of the implements is going up, at least some of the agents are working on a fixed amount as commission per unit. Anything I have to say will therefore be directed at the implement companies. A little over a year ago we were told by the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) that the big fellows were all set. I believe these implement companies are included with the big fellows. I believe an investigation, a royal commission if you like, should be set up to deal with these matters. The prices for fertilizer, binder twine and many other such commodities are far too high. An investigation into one of these commodities would help bring down the prices of the others.
In 1950 the farmers of the prairie provinces had a really tough time. Their crops were snowed under without much being harvested. A similar situation obtained in 1951. I am not going to deal with that. This afternoon the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) gave an outline of what is being done, and the quantities of grain that are still under the snow. I imagine the farmers who will harvest in the spring will be wise enough not to commence harvesting until their grain is in prime
216	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Fair condition. Many millions of bushels of grain that are now in the granaries or in piles on the ground will be in danger of spoiling as soon as the warm weather commences because of the moisture content of that grain. This is not a matter for the farmers alone, because labour depends upon the ability of the farmer to purchase the products of the factory. The businessman should also be interested in this problem. While the price of agricultural products has been dropping for the last few months, not all of the decrease has been passed on to the consumer. Some of it has been, but not all by any means, so that again the farmer is taking the rap, as suggested by the Rural Co-operator editorial.
There are other matters that I should like to deal with but I see that my time is fast vanishing. The cost of living index has decreased from 191-5 to 190-8 in January, and some of the things responsible for that decrease are as follows: a drop in the price of eggs, beef, pork, lard, shortening, men's woollen apparel, women's nylon hosiery, furniture, wool blankets and so forth. Practically all of these things have their origin on the farms, so that again the farmer is taking the rap. When computing percentages I am sorry that agriculture was still in the depression stage, back in 1939, and these figures have been used in making the comparison, and that was the disaster period for agriculture.
In conclusion I want to say that because of the fact that member nations of FAO, including Canada, turned down recommendations for the setting up of a world food board or commodity clearing house, Canada should take immediate steps to expand sales of food to Europe by either accepting imports in return for her exports or accepting their currency to be used for either future purchases or investments.
Canada should support international food agreements in order to assure Canadian farmers that if they expand production of food there will be a market for it, and that the price be tied to the general price level in the importing countries. At the time of the British wheat agreement we warned that the result would be that European nations would be unable to buy our goods. The government should revise administration of income tax legislation so that it will not discourage an increase in production. In order that these things may be brought about, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch):
That the following be added to the address:
We regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed:

(a)	To provide adequate inducements for the possible and essential expansion in the production of foods in Canada, and
(b)	To provide for the economic marketing and distribution of whatever part of our food production may become surplus.
If present conditions are the best our government can provide, then I suggest that Social Credit proposals be given a fair and honest trial, in the interests of all the Canadian people.
