speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, along with other hon. members, want to congratulate the mover (Mr. George) and the seconder (Mr. Gauthier, Lake St. John) of the address, and I sincerely congratulate them on having done a first-class job.
I would like to appeal to the government at this time and ask them to hurry up the legislation dealing with the War Veterans Allowance Act. I know a large number of old gentlemen who are suffering from the delay. While I think that the legislation should have been brought in last year-I should like to have seen it last year-I hope that the government will now hurry up and bring it in so that these elderly citizens, who served this country faithfully, will get the benefit of it.
I have another matter that I should like to bring to the attention of the government. It concerns my own constituency, and in particular the Roblin park subdivision, which was set up under the Veterans Land Act. These homes have been equipped with a septic tank disposal system. A serious condition has existed there over the past five years regarding the inadequacy of the septic tank system of the various veterans homes to function during the wintertime. Representations have been made to the Veterans Land Act administration at Winnipeg at different times, complaining that this situation should be corrected. But I think the main drawback, up to the present time, has been that they have never had sufficient funds available to spend in the improvement of the system or the rectifying of it.
The situation this year has been aggravated no doubt by the light snowfall and the Californian weather that we have had in Manitoba. We hear of many septic tanks being frozen which have never been frozen before. That may be one factor in the case, but this complaint is by no means new in this district. They have had frozen septic tanks for the past five years; that is, since the subdivision was set up, and every year it is becoming worse. The land, which is a heavy gumbo soil, is not the best land to have disposal fields laid in, and the construction needs particular care to see that there

is sufficient gravel laid into the fields. I have a petition on my desk, Mr. Speaker, from 50 householders of that area who are up against this problem.
When I left Winnipeg ten days ago, 64 of the homes on that subdivision out of 90 houses had their septic tanks frozen up. The argument has been used at different times that some of the men did not take the necessary precaution of covering their fields with straw. I have interviewed men there who have complied with all the good advice handed out by the Veterans Land Act administration, and still their disposal systems have frozen.
These homes were bought by these veterans on the understanding that they would have a plumbing system that would work. I consulted with the provincial sanitary authorities, and they assured me that if these disposal fields are properly laid they will give good satisfaction up to 25 years, without being interfered with.
One thing drawn to my attention by some of these men is that some of the fields have not been properly laid; that is, each disposal field should have had so many cubic yards of gravel. Some of the men who have had to dig up and re-lay their fields have found that there was no gravel there, and in others a very little amount.
A house in this district with a proper sewerage system is worth $1,000 more than a house without one. I appeal to the department and to the government to institute an inquiry into this and lay aside sufficient money to correct this situation. If the situation is not corrected we are certainly going to run into trouble. Can you imagine 64 men pumping sewage on top of the snow every second night of the week? The week I left for Ottawa it was quite mild, but you could detect the smell. What will it be like when the snow is gone or when spring comes? Is it any wonder that the women in the settlement are having their children inoculated against typhoid? How long will the provincial government sit back and let a state of affairs like this exist? Many have left this subdivision for no reason other than that the septic sewage under these conditions for one or two winters was all they could stand. Many more would like to leave, but they have put their money into the houses, and are unable to leave them. How long the provincial sanitary authorities will allow this to go on, I do not know. However, the act governing septic systems in the province of Manitoba, as published by the queen's
The Address-Mr. Bryce printer in that province, states in section 179 (1) (a) dealing with plumbing and drainage that-
No sewage or sewage effluent shall be discharged into a creek, river, lake or watercourse except in a manner approved and by and with the written authority of the minister.
The fluid from these 64 houses is just being pumped out into the snow. This section states that-
No sewage or sewage effluent shall be discharged into (b) the subsoil within thirty-five feet of any residence; or (c) on the ground surface within one hundred feet of any residence, or (d) into the subsoil or on the ground surface.
These conditions have existed for five years. While the provincial authorities may have been reluctant to do anything about it, the condition is becoming so bad that something will have to be done. The situation has become so serious that the government can no longer ignore it. I know that improvements have been made in other settlements that have been established by having one septic disposal tank for the whole system. I have in mind the West St. Paul subdivision. It may not be too late even at this time to correct the condition I have been describing. If there was one septic disposal tank for the whole settlement it might end the whole trouble.
Instructions issued by the Veterans Land Act administration have advised at times the cultivation of the land where the fields are laid, and later instructions have suggested that grass be grown over -the fields. But results up to the present time are that those who have lived up to all these instructions have had no better results than the ones who did not. I understand that in the first winter 38 of the tanks were frozen, and that they have been freezing in even greater numbers ever since.
Hence it is evident that there is something wrong with the construction. Homes where the owners have taken up the fields and put in the necessary gravel have had better results. But the digging up of the fields and the provision of a sufficient quantity of gravel is something that entails a considerable amount of expense to the owner. I feel certain that the government which sold the homes under the Veterans Land Act should see that these systems are made to work.. I do not think any hon. member would begrudge the appropriation of a small amount of money to put this sewage disposal system into proper working order. I do not wish to repeat what I have said already, but I would add that this is one of the finest subdivisions to be seen anywhere in Canada. The landscaping and other work these men have done is a credit to them. But when one visits

The Address-Mr. Bryce them in the wintertime and sees all this sewage being pumped into the back yards, he is confronted with an entirely different picture.
These men, who saw active service, know the value of sanitation in a community. I do hope that the Veterans Land Act administration is going to step into the picture and straighten out this matter before we have an epidemic of typhoid or some other fever. These men have asked me to tell the government about this condition and to ask that it be corrected. Their request is fair and reasonable. They bought homes which included a sewage disposal system; and if that system does not work properly, then I say it is only fair and reasonable to ask that the authority who sold the houses should put in a system that will work, or reduce the prices of the homes. For the government to sit back today and say that it has no responsibility is, I say, not good enough. I feel confident the minister will do the right thing for these men. I would urge that the matter be not laid aside any longer, but that immediate steps be taken to investigate the whole problem, with a sufficient amount of money appropriated to correct the condition.
Then, I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Veterans Affairs the situation now existing at Deer Lodge hospital in my constituency. Indeed, I live only two blocks from it. Employees at Deer Lodge received benefit of the recent increase in the salaries of civil servants. However, ward maids, kitchen maids and ambulance drivers did not receive the increase in pay, because apparently they are not recognized as civil servants. These employees are in the lower income bracket, and if any needed the raise, I should think they did.
I am sure this has been an oversight by the department, and I feel confident that the minister will have this condition corrected, so that no one can accuse the officials of discrimination. This would ensure harmony among the various employees of the hospital.
I would hope also that the minister might be successful in securing permission from treasury board to place a permanent building where the annex now stands. I was in that building once or twice when I was home in January, and I can say from experience that it is so cold that the water freezes. I know the government intends to do something about it but, thus far, nothing has been done.
I should like now to turn to another problem, namely the emergency situation in Canada today brought about by the serious outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease. I do not think anyone will disagree with me when I say it is an emergency situation, and one requiring drastic action. In my view we

should have a controller, or some other responsible federal authority, acting in conjunction with an advisory board composed of producers, consumers and processors, who would regulate the movement of cattle, and other matters connected with that industry.
Today in different provinces embargoes have been imposed. These will lead to a surplus of meat in some provinces, while in others there will be shortages. Some will be paying too much while others will be getting too little. A controller could regulate the movement of livestock in the present emergency. There is a lot of stock that will have to find its way to market in the near future. The country has to be fed. With the way things are at the present day, some provinces have too much meat while others have not enough.
Where there is a surplus of meat, the price to the producer will fall below the cost of production. Where there is a scarcity of meat, the consumer will not be able to pay the high prices that will be asked. I submit that in an emergency such as this there should be a controller who would control the price, both to the producer and to the consumer.
Under our system of free enterprise people sell for as much as they can get and buy as cheaply as possible. In an emergency such as this advantage can be taken by both sides. If a controller were appointed many hardships could be prevented. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture has expressed itself on this matter, and I quote from the Ottawa Citizen of this morning as follows:
Profit Through Tragedy
It would be "unfair" to ask livestock producers to bear the full brunt of it alone, the federation said in a brief presented to the cabinet. If meat prices fell "drastically," it would mean consumers were profiting by a "tragedy" which had befallen the producers.
The federation urged that the government support the beef and lamb market at prices prevailing a week before the outbreak was announced. This would protect the cattle industry and still provide these meats to consumers at a "considerably lower" price than they paid in January or at any time in the previous half-year, the federation said.
One week before the foot-and-mouth disease broke out the cattlemen were taking approximately 10 cents per pound less than they had received a week before. That means practically $100 less per animal. The question that worries me is this: Has that drop in price been passed on to the consumer? It has not. A steer or cow will run about 1,200 pounds live weight and will dress approximately 50 per cent. If the price paid for the steer or cow was 30 cents per pound on the hoof, that would mean about 60 cents per pound on the rail. The processor would have the head,

heart, liver, intestines, blood; in fact all the offal to pay for his services. If the price for the cow or steer drops to 20 cents, the beef should be worth 40 cents and the consumer should be able to get his meat 20 cents per pound cheaper. In many cases the price to the consumer has dropped only a few cents, perhaps five cents or so. Apparently the retailer has increased his spread by 15 cents per pound.
Speaking in the house on previous occasions I have blamed the processors or packers for high prices, but when I spoke with the packers in Winnipeg I was assured that the retailer is the man to blame. I do not know whether that is the case, but I do know that when the price of cattle or hogs drops we find that that drop in price is not passed on to the consumer as it should be.

I do not know to what the hon. gentleman refers. I am ready to back up 100 per cent anything I have said in the house. I have been thirty-two years in this business and without wanting to be boastful or proud I do submit that when I speak in the house I speak about things about which I know something.
As I say, I was told by the packers just what these retail spreads were and I was astonished. I had mentioned that these drops in price are not passed on to the consumer as they should be. The farmer has always been blamed by the consumer for the high price of meat, but that is not the case. Along with my colleague, the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), I endeavoured to have an investigation made into the meat packing industry, but the combines people did not think that there was any room yet for complaint.
On a previous occasion I referred to the price of pork and I showed how the farmer was taking $18 less per hog than he had received in August, whereas the price of pork to the consumer had dropped only a few cents. Today the hog producer is facing ruin. I am glad that the Department of Agriculture has decided to make a change in the grades in order to protect the farmer.
I appreciate what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has done in the way of allowing for a heavier carcass. But that will help only the first grade, the A bacon grade; anything heavier will be no better than sows, and sows have been priced at 11 cents on the hoof these last few days.
I do not know what the producers are going to do unless they are allowed to move their animals quickly. That is one reason
7, 1952
The Address-Mr. Catherwood why I suggest that a controller should be appointed at this time. A man should have the right to move his hogs to market when they reach a weight of 250 pounds. As many hon. gentlemen know, you can put on two pounds a day and before you know it you will be selling only lard.
There should be someone in charge of this situation so that the consumer will get his meat requirements at a reasonable rate without exploitation by anyone and the producer be protected from unnecessary losses so that when the emergency is over he will be in position to continue supplying food to Canada.
I have not said anything about dairy products, but they will come into the picture if this disease spreads. It may affect the supply of milk to towns and cities or to cheese factories. Some farmers make a specialty of feeding lambs and if there is a shortage of feed, they will be hit quite hard. I have given the whole problem serious and careful consideration from both the producer and the consumer point of view. It is an emergency and should be handled by a federal authority. I know each province means well and wants to run its own business, which is their right. Therefore I want to move, seconded by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright):
That the amendment be amended by adding thereto the following paragraph:
"(c) To establish a federal authority to deal with meat and with dairy products during the present emergency, with power to establish floor prices for producers, to protect consumers by control of retail prices, and to arrange for the equitable distribution of such products during the said emergency.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. George) and the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Gauthier) on their speeches in moving and seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne. It is an honour that is given to two members of the government party at each session of parliament, and I feel they have acquitted themselves very ably indeed. I should also like to extend my congratulations to the newly appointed Postmaster General (Mr. Cote). I trust he will carry out effectively the duties and responsibilities he is now assuming.
The speech from the throne gives us an opportunity to discuss matters that are near and dear to our hearts, and I feel that this time-honoured privilege of the members of the Senate and the members of the House of Commons is one that we should maintain. I took advantage of the opportunity afforded

The Address-Mr. Catherwood by the recess to read all the speeches made last session in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I read them very carefully and I can say that I found something of interest in all of them which would be beneficial to the government if put into effect. Therefore I trust this time-honoured custom will not be curtailed too indiscriminately. I realize there are many people who feel that in the debate on the speech from the throne there is a repetition of many points in the speeches. That is true but I feel such repetition is necessary in many instances in order to force the government to take action on matters that we believe are of the utmost importance to the people of Canada.
It is rather early in the debate following the speech from the throne to analyse properly the contents of the speech, but upon reviewing it, and realizing how impossible it would be to include all the legislation it is planned to bring before the house, I feel nevertheless, as my leader pointed out yesterday, that it is perhaps more notable for what it does not contain than for what it does contain. Many specific matters that we believe should have been mentioned in the speech from the throne were not dealt with. Personally I had hoped that the government would have been prepared to announce co-operation with the provinces in extending some form of aid to crippled and disabled people who are unable to earn a living for themselves. The need for this was brought forcibly to the attention of members of parliament two sessions ago. A group of these unfortunate people, representing as they did many more who were unable to come, came here and presented their case very well. We were all in sympathy with their claims and we had hoped that legislation would be brought in that would be beneficial to them.
We are very happy that the government of the province of Ontario has announced legislation to this end, and I feel they are to be commended highly. It is a great and humanitarian effort but I believe it is one that should be federal in scope and administration. While we in Ontario are particularly happy that a ray of sunshine will be brought into the lives of these people, there are still many thousands in Canada who need this assistance, and I trust the government will give consideration to co-operation with the provinces in this regard.
During the brief intermission between the closing of the fifth session and the opening of the sixth session of the house I, as I know many other members of parliament did, had an opportunity to visit many of the people in my constituency. One of the things that

warmed my heart more than anything else was to go into a number of homes where they were receiving the old age pension for the first time and to see the happiness that has come to these people. One thing is certain, Mr. Speaker. Communism will never rear its ugly head in these homes where the pension is coming in regularly. I was most happy to feel that the Progressive Conservative party had played a very important part in making that legislation possible.
I do say, however, and I emphasize this very strongly, that there is a limit to the amount of taxation which the people of the country can bear. I agree with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when he pointed out yesterday that the limit had been reached but I also say it has been passed. The government must realize more seriously than ever before how dangerously we are riding the crest of an inflationary spiral. The time has come when we in this parliament, and the government particularly, have got to consider retrenchment because the days of buoyant revenue will not be with us to the extent they have been during the past year.
I also feel that the surplus we built up during the past year has not been in the best interests of the people of Canada. Perhaps that does not coincide with the views of many members of the house, but this huge amount of money that has been built up by the government has created hardship among many people throughout the land. We know of many industries which at the present time are having difficulty in carrying on owing to the burden of heavy taxation. I should like to refer to an article in the Financial Post of March 1, 1952, respecting the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. It reads as follows:
Bell needed additional net earnings of approximately $6,500,000 to meet obligations to shareholders . . . That would mean a modest boost in current rates . . .
The article goes on to point out, however, that they have to collect $14,400,000 to cover the extra taxes on the higher earnings. That is only one company of many in this country that are in a similar position. In reading the financial reports of many other companies we see that a similar situation exists, and therefore we must realize that the limit of taxation has been reached.
I am sure all members of parliament are concerned about having good, sound legislation, and I believe most members will support legislation of this kind when it is brought before this house. So I think at this time the government must measure its expenditures more carefully than ever before. We

must realize that the defence expenditures to which we have committed ourselves must be made; and in that connection we were happy to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) announce that a committee will be set up to scrutinize those expenditures. I believe the committees of this house have a very important job to do. On them much depends and if the government will co-operate with those committees and make available all necessary information, we will have better legislation and get better value for our dollars. As a result we may be able to reduce some of the burdensome taxes that have been imposed.
This afternoon the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) outlined the position of the textile industry in this country. I highly commend him on his effort, which I believe should be supported by all those who recognize the importance of this great industry to Canada. For the past twenty years, as he pointed out, one worker in twelve in this country has been closely associated directly or indirectly with that industry. This has been a great stabilizing influence in our economy, and we realize how important it is that we keep the textile industry prosperous. Harold Smith, who was president of the textile association, said in 1950 that the market continues to shrink, and as long as that goes on it will be necessary to have reasonable protection for this industry. His opinion was shared by the minister of trade and commerce of Australia, who pointed out that we must protect our textile industry from dumping and also from excessive imports. Our own Minister of Trade and Commerce, speaking to the textile industry some time ago, pointed out how important it was to the people of Canada to keep that industry flourishing, and I am very glad he has recognized that fact.
We have a peculiar situation in this country. The demand for textile products is at an all-time high, yet the industry has never been more depressed than it is today. Other countries are also concerned about the importation of cheap textiles. Speaking in the House of Lords not long ago Lord Barnby came out very strongly against the importation of Japanese textiles to such an extent that the whole industry was depressed. He also made reference to the position of Canada, pointing out the serious unemployment that has developed in that industry here. South Africa faces the same situation, and the board of trade has spoken very strongly about the importation of textiles into that country. This matter is of great concern and, as the hon. member for Lanark pointed out this afternoon, serious consideration should be
The Address-Mr. Catherwood given to all aspects of the textile trade. I hope the Minister of National Revenue will give it his attention, so that we may maintain one of the oldest and best established industries, which has been a mainstay of the economic life of many of our towns and villages. I know of many cases where a textile mill is the only industry in a town or village. So we must not allow things to get worse and the industry to become completely demoralized. The textile industry is operated as efficiently as any other industry in Canada, I am sure, and it only asks for sufficient protection to give it a fair share of the home market.
Now, sir, I would like to turn very briefly to agriculture. This afternoon the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) referred to the tobacco industry of Canada. He also mentioned something that is important to this house, when he discussed the letter which he read to us referring to the action of a certain tobacco company. I am sure none of us would support actions of that kind; but I do feel that the tobacco producers should be given some consideration. A delegation from the flue-cured tobacco marketing association met the minister in January of this year. That was the second time they brought their problems to him, pointing out how necessary it was to drastically reduce taxes, particularly on cigarettes. They asked that taxes be reduced to the point that a package of twenty cigarettes would sell for 30 cents, which would still be 50 per cent higher than in the United States. The minister listened carefully to the delegation, but gave no indication that he would favourably consider their request. I do trust that in the interests of justice, of sound reasoning, of our national economy and of a great segment of our agricultural population the minister will consider reducing this most burdensome, unpalatable, depressing and intolerable tax in line with the request of the association.
This taxation has caused a new industry to spring up along our border, what we might call the smuggling corporation of America. This is a very serious business, and sometimes I think many hon. members do not realize to what extent these tobacco products are brought in illegally. This industry is operating, but is contributing nothing to our national revenue. Nor is it contributing anything to the morale of our people. It is making many of our citizens parties to illegal acts, in that they are purchasing these smuggled cigarettes. I am afraid that business will continue to flourish as long as we continue this excessive taxation. I am sure the minister himself must be anxious to clean up this situation. We know the smugglers are very

The Address-Mr. Catherwood happy today, and I think it is up to this government and this parliament to see that they are made most unhappy.
During the last few days we have had a searching debate on the most dangerous disease ever to threaten the livestock industry of Canada. The gravity of the situation is such that great anxiety has been created in the minds of our people. The loss of the great American market will affect directly or indirectly all fourteen million people of this country. A major catastrophe such as this cannot help but have far-reaching consequences to the economic life of our people. This emphasizes what can happen when we build up trade with one country and neglect our trade with other nations. The great agricultural industry of Canada was built on the export trade; and the action of the United States in prohibiting the importation of cattle, hogs and dairy products, for which we cannot blame them, should forcibly recall to this government the many speeches made by members of the opposition parties in this house on so many occasions on the need to seek other avenues of trade. I feel that the government should recognize this fact and give it close attention.
This afternoon the member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) pointed out that we do need this trade, and that we should avoid placing a dependence on trading principally with one country. Hon. members will recall that on February 28, 1950, the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) moved that:
. . . this house is of the opinion that the government should take immediate steps to convene at the earliest possible date a conference of the nations of the British commonwealth and the countries of the empire to devise policies to restore our lost markets, and thereby to provide jobs for our Canadian people.
Following the debate upon that resolution, the question was put to a vote and it was defeated by the solid vote of the government against the vote of the combined opposition parties. At that time we thought it was most unfortunate that this motion was rejected, as it closed the door more tightly against the possibility of increasing our trading relations with the empire nations. However, I do not believe we should dwell on the past mistakes of the government, but I do believe the government should benefit by those errors in judgment and be prepared to amend their ways.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) stated this week that every effort would be made to locate new markets for our meat and dairy products. I suggest to him that he sincerely investigate the possibilities suggested by the member for Lake Centre. Although that resolution was moved two


years ago, the proposition is just as sound today as it was then. One thing is certain; no harm can come from such a conference, and good could result. We have lost our market south of the border, and it may be lost for some period of time. It may be that we shall never regain that market to the extent we had it this past year. I trust that the minister, who had remarkable success in persuading his colleagues to accept his advice and judgment in the past, will use his influence toward this end. Canada is a nation whose very existence depends upon export trade.

I should like to compliment the member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) on his statement this afternoon. If hon. members listened to his speech and the last one, they will have come to the realization that so far as the textile industry, the agricultural industry and other

industries in this country are concerned, there is no solution to their problems within this country. The problem is international. I thought that we had solved the problem when Mr. Churchill and the late Mr. Roosevelt made their famous declaration in the Atlantic charter. At that time they set out a five-point charter which suggested that when this war was over it would be necessary to recognize the fact that we were living in one world and were interdependent. When the war was finished we were to sit around a conference table and open our borders to a free exchange of raw material, with some regulatory body deciding to divide up the economic resources of the world on the basis of need. This has not happened. Apparently, that was only a document to take us on another step into the war. When the war was over, this document became a declaration of principles without any legal effect. No one has done anything about it. As a result, the member for Lanark's case was one hundred per cent correct.
The hon. member showed the extent to which our people depend on that industry. He showed what the picture is in other countries, the international competition and the difference in wage rates in the different countries. There is no possibility of reconciling that difficulty within this country, within Britain or any one country. The same situation applies to our agricultural products. We can run around in circles setting up tariff barriers, but the problem is world wide. I do not think we have followed to the extent we should the purpose for which the United Nations organization was set up. There is no solution within any one country, and unless the problem is tackled on that basis I do not think there is very much we can do about it.

The Address-Mr. Gillis we discussed. I would say definitely that this throne speech gives me the assurance at least that we are not to fight an election this year.

speechtext:
No. Perhaps there were things that happened after the last throne speech was introduced that caused the government to change its mind. Well, that is permissible. If I were in the Prime Minister's place perhaps I would be doing the same thing. I am not criticizing that; I am merely giving my own impressions.
In my opinion this is a document that aims at tidying up a lot of legislation. There is one omission from it that I am rather sorry to see, but it is the one that convinces me that we are not going to have to face an election this year. It is the fact that the government not only has no reference in the speech to a national health program, but the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) has assured us also that it is not the intention of the government to set up a committee to study the matter. I believe that that is the most important issue in the country today.
I said that it looked like a tidying-up process. Perhaps that is good strategy at this time. Perhaps it is good strategy to pause and take a look at the field of social security and ascertain how much further we can go in that field. I believe that in this country today a national health program is an essential. I am rather disappointed that the government is not at least setting up a committee further to study the matter and relate it to the social security program that we have at the present time. It would give hon. members an opportunity to determine what the need was, how well equipped the provinces are to handle it, and what the total cost would be in that regard in tying in that essential national health program with the social security measures that we have at the present time. I think that is the next step in the field of social security. But, as I said before, in my opinion this will likely be saved as an issue in the next election campaign.
I am convinced that we have to take a look at this whole social security program, because it seems that in curing one problem here and there we always raise another one. Most of us assumed, when the bill went through the house abolishing the means test at the age of 70 and dropping the age limit down to 65, that we had for the time being at least solved that problem of old age security. We have not solved it, not even in the age 70 group, because we have created

The Address-Mr. Gillis new problems by running into other legislation. When we say that we have removed the means test at the age of 70 it is not quite true. If you are a millionaire you can make application at the age of 70 and your income is not taken into consideration. That is not true when the incomes of others who are on other pensions are affected. For example, people who draw the blind pension as of right and who make application for the old age pension at age 70 are advised by the provinces-at least by the province of Nova Scotia-that they are transferring them from the blind pension roll to the roll of old age security. The blind pension which they were receiving they were entitled to because they were blind. They were entitled to it as of right. They are also entitled to the old age security pension at age 70 as of right, but we inject the means test again by considering the income received from the blind pension board. They are removed from that and are put on the old age security roll. In my opinion by doing that you are reintroducing the means test for that person who is afflicted and has that small income of $40 per month because of that affliction. I myself think that we have to take a look at that and ascertain if we have not overlooked that particular application of the means test to a person whose income is very small, and who is badly afflicted.
Another place where we run into it is in regard to the war veterans allowance. The War Veterans Allowance Act still contains a means test. After the recipient of a war veterans allowance, who may have been receiving it for years as his only source of income, reaches 70 and applies for the old age security, he is immediately notified that his income from the war veterans allowance is affected. That is not only retaining the means test in the War Veterans Allowance Act, but it is applying the means test on the basis of income under the Old Age Security Act, and it is a misnomer to say that we have removed the means test completely at age 70. While the millionaire's income is not affected, the smaller pensioner, the blind pensioner and the war veterans allowance pensioner are affected because they have $40 a month income from another source.
Another section of the Pension Act is affected. The disability pensioner is not affected. But take as an example a widow in indigent circumstances who had a son killed overseas. Suppose she has been granted a compassionate pension of $60 a month because of the loss of a son who would now be her support had he come back. As soon as she reaches the age of 70 and makes application for old age security she is immediately
[Mr. Gillis.I

notified by the pension board that her income is affected and will be reduced by $40 a month. There are these three particular classes. In my opinion they are classes that are the hardest hit of any section of our society because they are all receiving that little bit of income of $40 a month owing to their affliction. I refer to the blind pensioner, the war veterans pensioner who is broken down and in adverse circumstances, and the widow who is in indigent circumstances and was receiving a compassionate allowance. Someone should take a look at these three classes. Not much money is involved, but a very important principle is involved as applied to the removal of the means test from the Old Age Security Act.
I hope someone in authority, perhaps the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) when he is preparing his budget, might take a look at that, and see if we cannot clean out those sore spots, and really give us an old age pension at the age of 70, without any reference to income.
Then, the age of 65 is another spot where I believe we are going to have a good deal of difficulty. It is necessary for the provincial governments to pass the enabling legislation. As yet, some of those provincial governments have not passed legislation, with the result that there are thousands of people across this country who are greatly confused. I may be a person of 65 years, or 68 years, with proof of birth. I have made application. And perhaps I should point out that I am talking only about some unnamed person who has made application.

Many of them come to visit me, and I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has had similar visits. If I am such a person, we will assume that I have made my application. The law has been passed by the federal government. But these people who visit us do not understand that the provincial governments have not passed the necessary enabling legislation. The result is that they are badly confused as to when they will receive the pension. They think someone is gypping them.
As for the provinces paying the additional money, I can only say that it is difficult to see how some of the provinces in Canada can afford to pay it. When we take a look at provincial incomes across this country we see that provinces like Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia and, with a struggle, perhaps

one or two others, could pass such legislation with the assurance that they have the necessary revenue to foot the bill. But there are others who cannot do that.
The people in this age group, as between province and province, are entitled to equality of treatment. If a provincial government is not able to meet the bill, and cannot raise the necessary revenue, then I think it becomes the obligation of the federal parliament to consider what might be done in providing equality in that field. If help is necessary, then I think the matter should be taken into consideration.
That is another angle of the social security program that should be considered. I believe it might be considered appropriately at the time of the revision of the dominion-provincial taxing agreements which, I believe, expire at the end of this month. It can be readily understood that you cannot have equality in any of these services as between province and province when, in one province, there is a provincial income of only $15 million or $20 million while in another there is an income of over a billion dollars.
The provincial government with the smaller income cannot treat its citizens as they should be treated. I have never taken the position that I wanted to cling to the sovereignty of a province, and that I am entitled always to what was written into the constitution seventy years ago under the conditions then existing. I do not think we should cling to any principle of neglecting the poor in any province because of some theoretical nonsense of provincial rights. What I want is equality as between citizen and citizen in the Dominion of Canada. And if it is necessary to amend the constitution in order to preserve the interests of the people in any province, then I am prepared to amend the constitution without any regard for the feelings of any person in any province who thinks he has to retain the sovereignty of that province, as he sees fit. I am prepared to see the constitution changed. I believe that in order to have equality as between province and province it will be necessary to amend the constitution.
I should like now to say a few words about this very important amendment of the hon. member for Selkirk. This is a serious matter, and one we should think about for a few moments. He has said that this matter of the marketing of our cattle is a national emergency. I agree with him that it is. Not only is it national; it is an international emergency.
Most of our beef is produced in western Canada, where the disease has broken out. Immediately upon its breaking out, the United 55704-15
The Address-Mr. Gillis States, one of our export markets, declares an embargo against Canadian cattle. Then, as between province and province in Canada other embargoes are set up. This means that 80 per cent of the cattle industry which supplies beef to Canada and for export to the United States is tied up in two provinces.
As the amendment suggests, this means there will be a great surplus in that section, and that in those provinces prices -can fall away below production costs. It means also that because of a shortage in the other provinces that, to a large extent, were supplied from that source, prices can skyrocket.
I do not think we have any national machinery today that could handle the problem. First of all, in my opinion the people of this country received a scare in the last couple of weeks. Very little is known by the public about the disease, with the result that the average person will be reluctant to accept beef until he has been assured that the beef has been properly scrutinized. Or, if there is a lifting of the embargo as between province and province, the people will want to know that the cattle have been properly inspected, and that competent authorities have declared it free from the disease, free from contamination and fit for human consumption.
I do not think there is in existence any machinery that could give that assurance. The machinery being used at the present time is that which allowed this -condition to develop, and which permitted delay between the time of diagnosis -and the time when efforts were made to stop the spread of the disease. The hon. member for Selkirk h-as quite properly suggested the setting -up of a board- of competent people in the industry, headed by a controller with the right to supervise the industry's rehabilitation-because we know it has to be rehabilitated.
I have said this is an international question-and- it is, in more respects than one. Not -only is it international because the Americans have declared an embargo against our cattle, but it is international because the -disease itself is international. A couple of nights ago I listened to a broadcast from an authority from France. He characterized the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease as a world cataclysm. He pointed out that Great Britain has had- a large number of outbreaks since 1945, and that in that country it has not yet been eliminated. It has been isolated to certain sections. Then, he pointed out that France was polluted with it, that the whole of Europe was suffering from it, that they had it in the Argentine and in Mexico, -and that it was just beginning to appear in the Dominion of Canada.

The Address-Mr. Gillis
In view of the fact that they have been struggling against it for years in the countries I have mentioned-, and have not yet brought it under control, I believe we should take immediate steps to select the most competent people in the country and give them the authority to do a scientific job of regulation, so that the difficulty may be brought under control as soon as possible.
I believe that action of that kind- by the government at this time would give the people of Canada an assurance that these embargoes are not likely to continue, that infected cattle will not be permitted' to contaminate other animals, and that the meat available is fit for human consumption. In view of the fact that it has not been stamped1 out or brought under control by the other countries I have mentioned1, I believe the government of this country should take the steps recommended in the amendment for the purpose of developing machinery charged- specifically with the responsibility of handling this problem.
The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) made a good argument in connection with prices and stated that he had changed his opinion that the packers were entirely responsible for the high cost of meat. I think it shows considerable intellectual development when a man indicates he has changed his opinion. A wise man changes his mind once in a while but the fool goes on forever. The hon. member has indicated that he is a wise man. He consulted with the packers and got the facts. He ascertained that a great deal of the price fixing and the cost of high prices was to be found in the retail end.
My wife does all our shopping so I do not keep track of meat prices very much, but I do know that in some sections of the country retailers form associations and fix prices. Owing to recent advances in beef costs it has been found! necessary to revise retail prices.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw the attention of the government to the very serious situation which increasing unemployment is causing right across this country today. Many towns and cities are faced with the same problem that is facing my own city of Toronto, so I am going to use the situation that exists there as an example of what is happening in many other centres in Canada.
In Toronto, on February 21, there were 32,000 unemployed persons registered with
The Address-Mr. Hees the national employment service. This compares with 13,500 registered one year ago. I believe an increase of 140 per cent during the past twelve months shows that the local and national unemployment problem is becoming increasingly serious, and can no longer be ignored by this government.
Of the 32,000 unemployed persons registered in Toronto on February 21, some 80 per cent were eligible for unemployment insurance. Unfortunately, many of those people suffered extreme hardship for one or more of the following reasons:
First, a delay, often amounting to several weeks, between the date of application and payment of the first insurance benefits;
Second, the inadequacy of the benefits to provide for those with large families;
Third, the limited period for which benefits are paid. When benefits stop there is no other means of support.
So far I have been dealing with the 80 per cent who were eligible for unemployment insurance. The remaining 20 per cent, who were employable but who were not under the unemployment insurance scheme, had no means of support whatsoever. These people were in a most desperate plight.
Those who were not covered by the unemployment insurance scheme, or who were inadequately covered by it, have been fed and sheltered by the city, the Salvation Army, the Scott Mission and other charitable institutions. In most cases this has alleviated actual hardship and suffering, but in no way can it be considered a permanent solution. What these unemployed people want are jobs to work at, so they can provide for their families, and retain their self-respect. If it is impossible to find jobs, they want adequate unemployment insurance to tide them over until jobs can be found.
We may well ask ourselves why unemployment is growing at such an alarming rate, at a time when we should be enjoying peak prosperity and employment. It is due solely to the plundering and blundering of this government. They have plundered the people by overtaxing them to such an extent that they can no longer afford to buy the goods and services they would otherwise be buying. This has reduced production, and thereby reduced employment. They have blundered by imposing credit restrictions, designed to stop the purchase of civilian goods in order to make way for defence production, and then have not placed defence orders to take up the slack. The natural result has been unemployment.

The Address-Mr. Quelch
The logical answer is for the government to correct the mistakes it has made, and thereby restore production and employment to a normal level. However, this government will never admit or correct a mistake, so we must prepare for increasing unemployment as a result of these policies. Naturally, the coming of spring will ease the unemployment situation to quite an extent, but we can expect the present picture to reappear by next November, and perhaps a lot sooner.
If we are to avoid the experiences of the past few months, the time to do our planning is now.' These plans, I believe, should take the following form.
First, the unemployment insurance scheme should be extended to include a larger proportion of those not yet covered.
Second, unemployment insurance payments should be increased to compensate for the rise in the cost of living.
Third, the period between the date of application and the date of the first payment should be kept to a maximum of five days.
Fourth, when eligibility has been established, cash payments should be made immediately if it can be shown that an emergency exists within the family.
Fifth, until a permanent plan has been worked out between the federal, provincial and municipal governments, the federal government should assist the municipalities in paying the relief costs which have been made necessary by the inadequacy of the present unemployment insurance plan.
I believe it is about time this government tackled the unemployment problem in a realistic way, instead of simply pretending that it does not exist.
