Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne stresses the need to increase the combined strength of the nations of the free world in order to achieve a lasting peace by discouraging acts of aggression. However, it has been pointed out time and again by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and many others that we cannot hope to defeat communism by force of arms alone, but that we must take energetic action to increase the economic well-being of many groups of people throughout the world. However, in supporting that idea I would not say for one moment that poverty is the only cause of war. I believe there are many other causes, such as ideologies and the lust for power. But on the other hand, I am satisfied that we can never hope to achieve a lasting peace as long as we have
IMr. Hees.]
large scale starvation in any part of the world. When you have that condition, you have fertile ground for the spread of communism.
Unfortunately, up to the moment little progress has been made in solving that problem. I realize that we have the special agencies of United Nations Organization, FAO, technical assistance, the Colombo plan; we have had UNRRA and the Marshall plan; I think we would all admit that what has been accomplished by those agencies merely represents a drop in the bucket as compared with the tremendous problem that faces us. No doubt the increased tempo of defence will still further aggravate that problem, especially of course in Europe. To the extent that it does it may be said we are helping the nations behind the iron curtain, because they will be accomplishing their purpose if they can create increased discontent throughout the world. In that way, they hope to win support.
Today, over six years after the end of world war II, the problem of expanding the supply of food is one of primary importance. It is in that regard that I say we have made little progress. For instance, at the FAO conference held in Rome last November, the need for greater production of food was stressed time and again. I was interested in a statement that appears in the February issue of "External Affairs" on page 56, under the heading of "Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations," and I should like to quote the first paragraph:
Within the last century an acute new problem has developed in mankind's age-old struggle for subsistence. Progressive application of scientific knowledge to the problems of providing for material human needs, together with the rapid spread of social reform, has resulted in a state of affairs in which the rate of increase of the world's population has outstripped that at which food can be produced. The last fifteen years have witnessed a twelve per cent growth in the population of the globe, but no more than a nine per cent increase in its production of food. The present population rise of one per cent per annum, when translated into figures representing human beings, reveals the startling fact that there are between fifty-five thousand and sixty thousand new mouths to be fed every day.
Then on the following page it states:
As a result of rapid increases in the population of the world, present per capita supplies of food are below the unsatisfactory prewar levels.
I think that statement, in itself, justifies my saying that we have made little progress. As a matter of fact, it may be argued that we have lost ground because today the per capita supply of food is less than it was prior to world war II.

One may well ask, what is Canada's answer to that challenge. Our delegate, the Minister of Agriculture, when addressing the FAO conference stated that there had been a falling off in the production of milk, pork and beef in Canada since the end of world war II. Furthermore, he stated that he was afraid there would be no increase in the production of meat unless some assurance could be given to the farmers that a market would be found for that increased production. I do not want to be charged with misrepresenting what he said, so I am going to quote his words. I am quoting from a speech he made to commission I, food and agriculture organization conference, at Rome, Italy, Friday, November 23, 1951. On page 2,
I read:
In short, we are producing about seven per cent more milk than before the war and about seven per cent less than during the war.
About pork, he said:
Canada has produced during the last five years fifty per cent more pork than for the last five years before the war. But she is producing thirty per cent less than she did produce for five years during the war.
In regard to beef, he said:
Canada is producing about one million head more beef cattle than before the war, and about one million head less than during the war.
Then, the minister went on to point out that that was not a very happy picture to present to the conference, but he said the condition in regard to cereals was better. He had this to say:
Our barley supplies are better than ever before, and our oat supplies above the long time average. These, together with our feed wheat position, make it possible to produce more meat and dairy products.
I should point out our surplus production of cereals and meat comes from western Canada. The soil there is of high fertility with the result that the securing of fertilizer is not a problem.
I am afraid this increased production of meat and dairy products will not materialize unless fears are removed from the minds of our farmers. The meat and dairy farmer has no assurance he could dispose of his surplus if it were produced. His experience suggests to him that there is no outlet.
That picture, Mr. Speaker, could hardly be called an encouraging one so far as the farmers are concerned.
When the Prime Minister spoke before the Canadian Federation of Agriculture at Montreal in January, he also stressed the need for expansion in the production of food. He admitted, on the other hand, that there were serious problems in regard to distribution, but he argued that an increase was necessary in order to promote peace and happiness in the world. However, I thought the important point was that he did not give one word of assurance to the farmers of
The Address-Mr. Quelch Canada that if they did increase the production of food there would be a market for it. I am going to quote the words that he said in regard to the increased production of food and the effect upon world peace. He stated:
I realize of course that there are serious problems of distribution as you were reminded by your president this mcfrning. But those in the world who are not so fortunate as we in this North American continent are becoming more and more aware of their poverty in relation to our plenty. It has been ably stated that "never before has the close relationship between food and peace, food and justice, and food and human happiness been so widely accepted". We can improve still further our farming methods and go on increasing our productivity and thus meet our own needs and do our share to meet that world problem.
In the light of that picture displayed by the quotation from "External Affairs", by the Prime Minister's speech and by the attitude taken by the FAO conference, it is interesting to note what developed at the annual convention of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture held at Montreal in January of this year. For instance, what was the advice given to that convention by the Minister of Agriculture? What was the advice given to that convention by Mr. Hannam, president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and former president of the International Federation of Agriculture Producers? So far as the minister was concerned, he refused to give farmers any advice as to what they should do. He stated he would outline to them today's picture, and then it was up to the farm organizations to use their best judgment concerning what should be done. In his speech he kept to that idea and did not give the farmers any advice. However, in the discussion period, when he was asked point blank by some of the farmers as to what the market situation would be in the future, he did become more explicit. I quote from the Western Producer of January 31. The press clipping is headed:	"Production program farmer's
responsibility, Gardiner says." In reply to a question the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) went on:
Warning farmers against embarking on highly stepped-up production of food for the domestic market, Mr. Gardiner said earnestly that it was true the government did want to see production up. But as long as Britain lacked1 the dollars to buy Canadian cheese and bacon and eggs he was not going to tell any farmer to produce more hogs, more eggs or more cheese. Every farmer should know as well as he did that if Canada produced 15 per cent more hogs the price would go down to the American price in the absence of an export market in Britain.
The question of international exchange was a matter for countries to settle. He wanted to see bigger export markets as well as anyone, but farmers might as well face facts as they existed.
The president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, Mr. Hannam, drew a clear

The Address-Mr. Quelch picture when he addressed the convention. He did not mince words. I hold in my hand a press clipping from the Western Farm Leader, dated February 1, 1952, which reads:
Hannam states commodity program essential.
To take the position that Canada and other advanced countries should produce to capacity because people somewhere need the product is a fine humanitarian point of view, but it is a theoretical and impractical one unless an international commodity program exists to organize and supervise distribution.
Then he went on:
"Without expanding export markets," said the president (and this had been emphasized at the FAO conference), "our producers, and producers in other exporting countries, are in a like position- can do little but ignore the plea of the recent conference, much as they recognize the world need, and desire the opportunity of helping to meet it.
"They know too well that expanding production-without any assurance of a market for the additional product is too great a risk because it can clog markets, undermine prices and agricultural economies." Without export markets, the effect of such a policy would be "the very opposite of that which the efforts of well-intentioned producers would be designed to achieve."
I was interested to note that when he spoke to the women at the convention of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture he told them that the farmers would be crazy to expand production in the face of the present situation. Let me quote his words, as given in the Rural Co-operator, January, 1952:
"If we have no machinery to take care of all this increased production we'd be crazy to go about it. It would undermine our present surplus market, depress our home market and ruin our entire agricultural economy. That's the stark truth of it, and we've got to be realistic enough to realize it," said Mr. Hannam.
The Prime Minister calls for an increase in production of food; FAO calls for an increase in production. We all recognize that if there is to be peace in the world there must be an increase in production. I am not criticizing the Minister of Agriculture or Mr. Hannam for placing the picture they did before the federation of agriculture because they were placing the facts before them, but I am criticizing most bitterly the government policy that makes such a picture possible. The government are to blame for that situation; I certainly would not blame the Minister of Agriculture. The Minister of Agriculture and Mr. Hannam now both support the idea for some sort of a world food board or an international commodity clearing house for the purpose of distributing, or holding and distributing surpluses to needy nations.
This question has been before FAO for the last five years. Officials of that organization have from time to time submitted proposals to the conference of member nations, but unfortunately member nations have invariably voted down those proposals. Let me briefly review. The first proposal by FAO was for
[Mr. Quelch. 1
a world food board to buy up surpluses in times of plenty and hold and distribute them in times of scarcity. That seemed to be a sound proposal, but it was voted down by the member nations. The next proposal was for an international commodity clearing house. Again, this was turned down by the member nations, and it was voted against by Canada as well. It is very interesting to note the reasons given by the conference for turning down the proposal for setting up an international commodity clearing house. I hold in my hand the report of the conference as printed in the "International Federation of Agricultural Producers Bulletin", December, 1949. It is headed "Report of the Fifth FAO Conference" held in Washington, November 21*-December 7, 1949. It goes on to say:
In rejecting the short term trading functions of the international commodity clearing house, the conference observed:
(a)	That the accumulation of inconvertible currency would represent additional indebtedness by the deficit countries involving the burden of eventual repayment in terms of additional exports of goods and services and would have the effects of delaying the general convertibility.
What was the problem before the FAO conference? The problem was to bring about an expansion of the production of agricultural produce and provide for its distribution. Convertibility of currency can only be justified if it facilitates the carrying out of the problem. What do we find here? Here we find that a proposal to provide for an expansion of production and for its distribution was turned down on the grounds it might interfere with convertibility. In other words, they were confusing the shadow with the substance and the means with the end.
Speaking in this house on December 27 last year, I said that the Minister of Agriculture had voted against the international commodity clearing house on the ground that Canada could carry out the proposals contained in the international commodity clearing house for the purchasing and the holding of surpluses for their later distribution. The minister took exception to that remark and said that all he had been referring to was wheat, and definitely said that he had never suggested that Canada could do such a thing. Well, I did not make a statement like that without good foundation. I knew very well the minister had made such a statement, but unfortunately at that time I did not have a copy of his speech in the house. Therefore I am going to quote just exactly what the minister did say when he addressed the FAO conference at the time the international commodity clearing Louse was being considered. I have a copy of his speech here. I quote from page 5:
Canada, therefore, is prepared to give serious consideration to any international action designed to

attain production and distribution of food. From this point of view we are interested in the proposal advanced by the director general for an international commodity clearing house. While endorsing the principle underlying this proposal we are not in agreement with the means which, it has been suggested, are necessary to reach the objectives. In this connection we may appear to agree with what has been said by the United Kingdom and United States representatives.
Any transactions developed under the short term trading functions will be subject to concurrence by the governments concerned, and the major details of such transactions will also be subject to agreement by governments. This being the case it hardly seems necessary to havse an international agency actually buying and selling in commodity markets. It may even be questioned whether such activity in commodity markets by an international agency is desirable. It seems to us, therefore, that the question of the creation of a large capital fund for such a purpose is not necessarily an issue.
And later:
Lord Boyd Orr, in presenting his proposal for a world food board, had in mind the fact that the world had surpluses during certain periods and extreme shortages in other periods. It was his purpose to stabilize returns to producers and costs to consumers by setting aside surplus quantities in good years for periods of shortages. As has been pointed out in other conferences, however, national governments can, and do, perform this function and we do not see that stocks held by an international agency will, in the short run, contribute to any improvement in the present situation.
So Mr. Gardiner cannot see that it would help any for the international commodity clearing house to hold a fund for the purchase of these commodities. He considers that nations could just as well do it, and he cannot see that it would be necessary for the international commodity clearing house to buy up surpluses and hold them because he says that, in his opinion, national governments could do it. He did point out that Canada had indulged in such a practice in regard to wheat.
Now, coming back to my original point, that the problem of primary importance today is the expansion of the production of food, and the provision for its distribution throughout the world, we now find that the picture given by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and by the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is bound to lead to the conclusion that it would be unwise to expand production of certain foods in this country.
I remember some years ago when in this house we were discussing the United Nations organization some members suggested that the reason the league of nations had failed was because it did not have an army at its disposal. At that time I criticized that suggestion, and pointed out that to my mind the reason the league of nations had failed was not because it lacked an army, but rather because the nations who were members of 55704-16
The Address-Mr. Quelch the league lacked either the will or the sincerity to implement the policies that were essential to the maintenance of peace. I believe that is true in regard to the league, and I say it is equally true in regard to the United Nations organization. I doubt very much if the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) would deny that that is true, at least in so far as member nations behind the iron curtain are concerned. I would say it is also true in regard to Canada and the United States, because we recognize that one of the major problems is that of getting food to the people who need it. Yet we are not prepared to maintain in this country a policy which will make it possible for the farmers to expand their production.
And, as the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture said, under the situation as it is, farmers would be crazy to expand production of food. However, I am not prepared to accept the statement that unless an international food exchange is set up Canada cannot go all-out in expanding her production of food. Mind you, I favour the setting up of a body such as the international commodity clearing house; but if we are not able to get the friendly nations to agree to the setting up of such a body, then in my opinion Canada must be prepared to go ahead and provide for the expansion of her agricultural production. She must see to it that the production is distributed among the people who need it.
Mind you, I believe that that can be accomplished without creating a hardship for anyone. On the contrary I would say that a policy of that kind could very well still further expand the prosperity of this nation. I would say the first thing to do is to endeavour to expand the home market in Canada. It is all very well to talk about the difficulty of getting rid of the surplus in foreign countries, but are we certain that we have done everything in our power to expand the home market?
I am satisfied we have not, and I shall refer to that at greater length in a moment. Then, to the extent that we cannot market our produce in Canada, or exchange it for the goods of other nations, we must be prepared to sell our surplus to other nations in exchange for their currencies. And to the extent that those currencies cannot be utilized for the purchase of their goods, we must be prepared to invest those currencies within those countries in order to expand their production, so that they will be in a position to pay for their imports with exports.
There are two things to be considered in this regard. It may be that the nations to which we export goods have goods with which

The Address-Mr. Quelch to pay us in return, but which we are not prepared to accept. Or, on the other hand, it may be that their productive capacity is so low that they cannot produce the goods to pay for their imports. Then, in that case, where the productive capacity is low, and where we have exports that we are able to let them have, I think it would be our duty to invest the currencies that we receive from them to expand the production of such nations.
It may be asked: Would such a policy be burdensome on our people? The answer is no. This would not divert any capital from investment in Canada, because it would apply only to goods that could not be consumed in Canada, or exchanged for the goods of other nations.
Then, how should the Canadian government pay for these surplus goods? Well, so long as we have a surplus productive capacity in this country-for instance, so long as we have anywhere from 300,000 to 400,000 unemployed, men who could be used to increase the production of the country

and so long as we have expanding inventories, it seems to me that the purchase of surpluses to provide for investments abroad could be financed at least in part by the Bank of Canada.
To the extent that this might unduly increase inflationary pressure, it could be financed by borrowing the savings of the people. I think, however, the important point is that it would not be necessary to finance by taxation, because it would be a capital investment, and should be regarded as deferred consumption.
Furthermore it might be considered good policy to offset the heavy American investment that is taking place in Canada today by encouraging Canadian investment outside the country. So that in the future we will have wealth shipped into Canada on account of those investments to balance the wealth we have to ship out of Canada on account of the American investments in this country. However, as I said before, I am not satisfied for one moment that we are making the best possible use of the home market. I am satisfied that we are not developing the home market to the fullest extent, when I see in this country many groups of people enduring a very low standard of living.
For instance, when we have such people as old age pensioners living on $40 a month, can it be argued successfully that those people are consuming all they want to consume, or all they should be able to consume? We could very well increase their pension payments to $50 a month, and that $10 a month

extra would help provide a market for these surplus goods about which the Minister of Agriculture is so concerned.
Apparently the minister thinks it would not be safe for the farmers to expand production for the home market, because the market could not absorb it. Certainly we can take steps to expand the purchasing power of the low income groups in this country so that they can enjoy a healthy diet and at the same time provide a market for a proportion of these surplus goods.
In addition to those receiving old age pensions we have people who are incapacitated. They do not even get $40 per month. There is no provision of any kind made for these people. Surely no one can argue that a country such as Canada, a country which is worried as to what it will do with its surplus production, cannot afford to provide pensions for people who are physically incapacitated.
Then we have the recipients of war veterans allowances living on around $40 per month. Surely they could be paid $50 per month. That would help to increase the market for Canadian goods. I am very glad the government has indicated that the special committee on veterans affairs will be set up to deal with this matter. I do not think it is to the credit of this government that they have allowed these men to wait this long in order to get a standard of living to which they are entitled.
In addition to those whom I have mentioned, we have the unemployed and unemployables. No doubt if these people had a decent income today it would provide additional markets for our production. The additional demands by these people would all help to expand the home market.
I suppose that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) will suggest that such a policy would be inflationary. You cannot have it both ways. If we cannot expand production owing to a lack of markets, then expanding the home market will not cause inflation. It seems to me that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) indicated a somewhat confused state of mind when he spoke the other day on inflation and of the danger of increasing our imports from Great Britain. As reported on page 172 of Hansard of March 6, 1952, he said:
The most effective way would1 be to make more commodities available to be exchanged for the purchasing power distributed-and distributed so widely-among the public. I think everyone must agree that that is the only or, if not the only, certainly the surest way of combating effectively and of retarding inflation.
Then on page 174:
There again is a situation in which the one partial remedy would be the additional absorption

of British exports, or, from our point of view, British imports, in the Canadian market. We have had complaints from more than one quarter that some of our unemployment was the consequence of competition by imports from the British market that could not be met by our Canadian industries. That is also something that has to be taken into account. We have to look at the repercussions of these things on every segment of the Canadian economy. Can we increase our absorption of exports from the United Kingdom to any substantial degree without disturbing our own economy?
There again it seems to me that the Prime Minister cannot have it both ways. If, on the one hand, there are too many dollars chasing too few goods, then surely expanding imports from Great Britain should help to satisfy the demand of those dollars that are chasing around looking for something to buy. The Prime Minister says that we need more production in order to satisfy the demand of the surplus dollars, and on the other hand he argues that if we bring more goods into this country from Great Britain that may cause unemployment.
The Minister of Finance is quite fond of talking about too many dollars chasing too few goods. The situation that exists at the present time does not appear to justify that statement. On the one hand we have the Minister of Agriculture warning the farmers not to increase the production of agricultural products because if they do there may not be markets. Then we find the textile industry in a depressed state trying to find markets. Then we find inventories of many industries piling up. That does not look like too many dollars chasing too few goods. I am afraid the minister is too fond of painting such a picture so that he can get on his high horse and try to rope in more dollars.
I should like to say a few words about the prices of farm products. I am satisfied that if we want an increase in the production of agricultural products we will have to be prepared to maintain support prices at a proper level, a level which will give the farmer his fair share of the national income. I am perfectly well aware of the fact that many economists state that you cannot control prices. They say that to do so will mean running foul of the law of supply and demand. When people talk about the law of supply and demand it seems to me that they ignore completely the fact that the government by its action can affect both supply and demand.
The government by its policies can cause either an increase in production or a decrease in production. The government by its policies can cause either an increase in demand or a decrease in demand. So long as the government is in a position to bring about an expansion of production or a 55704-164
The Address-Mr. Quelch decrease, an expansion of demand or a decrease, it is in a position to maintain support prices.
Support prices should be established on the basis of parity. If that were done it would bring about an expansion of production. On the other hand1, if we are going to tell the farmers that they must be subject to the law of supply and demand we are not going to get increased production. Why? For the simple reason that if they are going to be subject to the law of supply and demand, every time the farmers expand their production in order to provide a reserve of food for needy nations, that state of affairs will be used as an excuse to force the prices of farm products down to a point where the farmers may receive less for their increased production than they were receiving previously. The natural result would be to discourage production.
It may be a fine humanitarian thing to say that the farmers should expand their production of food in order to feed the starving masses of the world. But the farmers want assurance that there will be markets for their production if they produce. In the past we have called upon the farmers to make sacrifices of many hundreds of millions of dollars in helping to subsidize the people of Britain and the people of Canada with cheap bread. It is time that we should be prepared to pay the farmers a price that will guarantee to them their cost of production and will bear a fair relationship to the prices they have to pay for the things they require.
The Minister of Agriculture has warned the farmers that if they expand production they are liable to be without a market. The president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has warned farmers that they will be crazy to take such action. The situation being what it is I intend to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) which reads:
That the following be added to the address:
We regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed:
(a)	To provide adequate inducements for the possible and essential expansion in the production of foods in Canada, and
(b)	To provide for the economic marketing and distribution of whatever part of our food production may become surplus.
I intend also to support the amendment to the amendment which reads:
That the amendment be amended by adding thereto the following paragraph:
(c)	To establish a federal authority to deal with meat and with dairy products during the present emergency, with power to establish floor prices for producers, to protect consumers by control of retail prices, and to arrange for the equitable distribution of such products during the said emergency.

The Address-Mr. Noseworthy

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne before us at the present time indicates that we shall have very little new legislation before us at this session and that much of our work will consist of the consideration of legis-latio namending statutes already on the statute books. Among the legislation that I am sure will be welcomed by the house is the proposed legislation pertaining to a further Canadian contribution to the Colombo plan and for technical assistance to underdeveloped areas. We can only hope that such assistance as is foreshadowed in the speech from the throne will be neither too little nor tdo late.
The house will certainly welcome much of the amending legislation mentioned in the speech from the throne, particularly that pertaining to the War Veterans Allowance Act. Many of us felt last session that when the basic pension to veterans was increased the veterans allowance should have been increased at the same time. It is encouraging to know that such increases as are to be granted this session will be made retroactive to the first of the year. I should like to point out that we sincerely hope that when that act comes before us for amendment there will be provision for one group of citizens not covered by the War Veterans Allowance Act. I refer [DOT] particularly to those in receipt of dependents' pensions, particularly those parents now growing old who are in receipt of pensions because of the loss in many instances of their only son who was at that time their main support. Upon inquiry at the office of the veterans allowance commission I could be given no assurance that even now the government contemplates increasing the pension to those dependents. I would certainly urge upon the minister the necessity of including that particular group along with those already in receipt of veterans allowance.
We shall welcome the amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Certainly experience in the administration of that act goes to show that very drastic improvements are needed, and before I take my seat I hope to dwell at some length on the nature of the improvements required. A subject of very grave concern to the people in my riding received very scant attention in the speech from the throne. I refer to the subject of unemployment. The only mention of employment in the speech from the throne was the very complacent remark that generally speaking employment remains at a high level. The fact that there were three or four hundred thousand Canadians ready

and willing to work and looking for work but unable to find it received very scant attention from the government.
Those three or four hundred thousand unemployed represent well over a million men, women and children who are deprived through unemployment of their weekly pay cheques. About 80 per cent of them were in receipt of the scant unemployment insurance payments. Some 200,000 Canadian men, women and children do not even receive the benefit of unemployment insurance. I think a matter which the government has failed to face seriously is the question of providing full employment for our people. As a matter of fact I think that neither this government, with its devotion to the free enterprise system, nor those national organizations which spend much of their time, energy and money in eulogizing the virtues of the free enterprise system, have yet faced up to the fact that that system in times of peace has utterly failed at any time in our history to provide the Canadian people with full employment. We were lifted out of the greatest slough of unemployment of all times by world war II. Only world war II enabled us to overcome the unemployment difficulties of the 1930's.
On the eve of Korea unemployment was again raising its ugly head and becoming a menace to hundreds of thousands of Canadian citizens. Once again it was the stark reality of war that enabled us to solve our unemployment problem for the time being. Once again during the past winter, notwithstanding the fact we are in the midst of a rearmament program, we were again faced with that recurring problem. We find three or four hundred thousand of our people unemployed. No wonder thousands of our people are asking today what would be the situation with respect to unemployment under this government if we were not in the midst of a rearmament program. Must we be forced to accept the theory that a Liberal government, a free enterprise government, can do nothing about unemployment except through the medium of military expenditure? That belief is growing in Canada. When the condition of unemployment, particularly in the Toronto area, was brought to the attention of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), he found satisfaction in the fact that the coming of spring would help us to rectify the situation. He assures us that the unemployment problem is a seasonal one, but it is a problem that has been recurring with the seasons. No effort has been made by the government and no plans have been provided to stave off unemployment-seasonal unemployment, if you wish. Early last spring it

was quite evident to anyone who gave any attention to the situation that during this winter we would be faced with large numbers of unemployed; yet no effort was made to remedy this recurring evil other than to rely upon unemployment insurance. We wait until our unemployment situation reaches its peak in midwinter; then we console ourselves with the fact that spring is coming and with it the unemployment situation will disappear. So we do nothing until the next season comes along. We forget about the unemployment which recurs each winter until it is upon us again.
That, I submit, just is not good enough for the Canadian people. If the free enterprise system cannot in and of itself provide full employment for our people, then it behooves the government, in the interests of those people who elected them, to take such steps as are necessary to supplement the efforts of the free enterprise system with a much needed and useful program of public works. Such a program should be ready long before the unemployment crisis comes upon us. Since last spring, when it became evident that we were going to be faced with unemployment this winter, this government has had ample time to make some provision whereby the slack in employment might be taken up. If they were not ready to absorb those unemployed people in the production of armaments then some other government project, much needed and useful in the interests of the community, should have been ready to be undertaken to keep our people employed during the winter.
First and foremost in any such public works program I think should be a low rental housing project. Dr. Firestone, the economic adviser to the Department of Trade and Commerce and also to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, as reported in the Globe and Mail of September 21 last, told a Toronto audience that in spite of the fact that from 1949 to 1951 we built close to
100.000	housing units each year, by 1955 we would need to build anywhere from 115,000 to 135,000 housing units per annum to catch up on our backlog. He assured us that at the end of 1951 some 500,000 Canadian families were still without homes.
The relation of such a building program to unemployment can be seen when it is realized that when we built about 90,000 housing units in 1949 we gave year round employment to
235.000	Canadians-and here I am quoting Dr. Firestone's figures-either in building the homes or in providing the necessary materials and services for those homes. According to Dr. Firestone the building of 135,000 housing units per annum would provide year round
The Address-Mr. Noseworthy employment for at least 300,000 Canadians. Had we this year been engaged in the building of 135,000 housing units instead of finding an actual reduction in the number built, many of the problems of our unemployed1 people would have been solved.
One of the best alternatives to military expenditure for the purpose of providing employment is the development of our resources and the building of homes for the Canadian people. Unless we are to get to the point where we have to depend upon either war or preparations for war to provide employment for our people, we must turn our attention to some of these projects which are needed by this country. If we are to do that I suggest we must first recognize that housing is a social matter. Housing is not something that can be considered primarily as a business activity. A report on housing prepared back in 1949 by the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities states at page 7:
We must keep on reminding ourselves that the purpose of housing is to house people and to house them in such a way as to encourage good family life and to provide them with the amenities necessary to health, welfare and good citizenship, even if, in order to do so, we must introduce public policies not normally associated with an economically operated business activity.
Housing in 1949 was the number one domestic problem facing the people and government of Canada, and in my opinion, that is still the case today. If we set as; our goal the provision of adequate housing for the Canadian people at prices they can afford to pay or, where they cannot buy, the provision of decent rental houses at rents they can afford to pay, we shall be moving constructively toward achieving a more certain full employment. Moreover we will be giving our people a very vital and real stake in our democracy.
The question may be asked immediately, what can the government do? As I have already said, I think we must first recognize that housing is a social matter; that our concern should be the welfare of the people and not the profits or security of the lending institutions of this country. This will involve releasing the government housing authority, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, from its bondage to the lending institutions of this country. Either do that, or relieve the lending institutions of some of the credit restrictions imposed on them by the government through the Bank of Canada. There is today a very wide market for homes that could be built, even at today's prices. There is the material and manpower available, but there are no finances.

The Address-Mr. Noseworthy
Only yesterday I read correspondence from two of the largest lending institutions in this country who said that they did not have mortgage money available for home building on any large scale. The best that they could advance to an individual builder was enough money to finance ten or fifteen units. I am told on good authority that the lending institutions in this Ottawa area this year had only about $600,000 of mortgage money available to put out for the building of homes under our national housing scheme. Everywhere throughout this country builders are finding it impossible to secure money to build homes for which the people are clamouring. These builders have the material and the manpower to do so, but because the finance companies have .such a stranglehold upon the government-operated housing authority, there is a bottleneck. I suggest that the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott)' get into a huddle to see if they cannot do something to make funds available to the builders to provide homes for our people.
Then, there is the question of just how much of our unemployment problem today is the direct result of the government's fiscal policy. There is no question but that the government's policy is directly responsible for the decline in home building. The government has not yet devised a policy that will meet that particular need. While the minister of resources is trying to get more houses built, the Minister of Finance adopts policies that curtail our building program. I think it is conceded by most people in Canada today, except possibly the cabinet and the manufacturers association or the chamber of commerce, that the government's fiscal policy designed to curb inflation is discriminating against the working class people in this country. I hear that charge against the minister's policy wherever I go, among the working class people.
On the one hand, the government allows prices to rise to unprecedented heights. On the other hand, they take away from the consuming public $700 million in surplus taxes for the purpose of reducing the spending power. Then, by additional excise taxes, sales taxes, credit restrictions, they price many of the necessities completely beyond the small purchasing power that is left to the ordinary low income people. Take the government's restrictions on automobiles-here I want to tell the Minister of Finance that this is not propaganda from the automobile dealers association, and I have not been approached by any automobile

dealers. No automobile dealer has held out to me the promise of free publicity or anything else in order to take up his case. In my own riding I have been approached by numerous working class people who want to buy secondhand cars in order to take their families out into the country or themselves to work, and who just cannot raise that fifty per cent down payment which the government's policy requires. I have received letters from numerous working class people in my riding who want to buy new washing machines for their wives, but those washing machines are priced beyond their reach because of the government's taxation policy. Apparently the Minister of Finance considers that a washing machine is a luxury. Let me assure him that in the working class home today it is no longer a luxury. These people in my riding who are being thrown on the unemployment market today because of the closing down of washing machine factories are blaming the government directly for the un employment.
The government has persistently refused over the years to impose price controls. It is rather an unusual circumstance to find that the only place where they impose direct price control is on the over-all price of a house, while at the same time they make no effort to control the price of the building material that goes into that house. Apparently the government is relying largely on its fiscal policy of high taxation and credit restrictions to curb inflation. In order to curb inflation, must we have unemployment thrust upon hundreds of thousands of Canadian citizens? Must we force hundreds of thousands of our people to go underfed through the long cold winter months in order to curb inflation? That is what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and his colleagues are actually forcing the Canadian people to do. Why must these sacrifices be imposed upon one class of people only? The man with money is not affected, or not seriously affected, by these credit restrictions. He can buy a new or secondhand automobile any time he wants to, or as many as he likes. He can buy as many electrical appliances as he likes. It is those in the low-income group who are being forced to pay that sacrifice by reason of this government's policy.
In his answer to a question that I raised here a few days ago the minister found considerable consolation in the fact that the majority of those unemployed people in Toronto were drawing unemployment insurance. I know, as he knows, and as every one of us knows, that these unemployment insurance benefits have proved a godsend to those hundreds of thousands of people who have been unemployed. There is no

question of that. But in a great many instances, even where the worker is in receipt of full benefits, the unemployment insurance is inadequate if a man with a family has to depend on the benefits alone. The maximum for the married man is somewhere around $21 a week. In the township of York the unemployment benefits are equivalent to the amount paid in relief to a family of three. Any man receiving unemployment insurance who has more than three in his family gets less from his unemployment insurance than he would get were he on relief in the municipality. A married man with a family of six would get $84 a month in unemployment insurance. In direct relief the municipality would pay $145 a month. Even if he has five or six children the man and his family must subsist on unemployment insurance amounting to approximately $84 a month.
When the minister considers amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act, I would suggest that the first thing to do, if at all possible, is to raise the weekly payment. The sum of $21 a week today just is not sufficient for a man with a family, particularly with today's prices. He just cannot subsist on it.
The second suggestion pertains to the waiting period. Theoretically a man must go one week before unemployment insurance comes into effect. Then he is supposed to have another week, or a total of sixteen days officially; nine days maximum from the time his unemployment insurance benefits start. Relief officers in Toronto and in York township have told me that they know of numbers of cases where men going on unemployment insurance have had to wait as long as 35 days before they were able to draw unemployment insurance. The Toronto offices are simply bogged down with the work of handing out unemployment insurance. I have gone into these offices. I have found the stairs jammed. The ones that I went into, the two that affect my riding, are on the second floor. I have seen the stairs jammed solid with people. If a fire ever broke out there is not the slimmest chance of any of these people ever getting out of these buildings. The upstairs floor was crowded. I have seen as many as 800 people crowded into that upstairs room. I have seen the stairs jammed and a line-up nearly a block long outside the building. These offices just cannot handle the amount of business that they have been called upon to handle during the past winter. There is no reason why people living as far north as Willowdale, or up in the northwest end of my riding, should have to come downtown to Spadina once every week in order to draw their unemployment insurance. There is no
The Address-Mr. Noseworthy good reason why we should not have an unemployment insurance office somewhere in the vicinity of Eglinton avenue, which would be within easy reach of people living in the north end of the city and the townships. It would save congestion at these downtown offices. The officers tell me that the business could be handled much more efficiently if it were more decentralized than it is at the present time.
I wonder whether the minister can tell us why the unemployment insurance people cannot do as the workmen's compensation people do in the province of Ontario. When a man can establish the fact that he is unemployed, instead of having to wait nine days, fifteen days or twenty days, why is it not possible to make some arrangement with the welfare officers in the municipality whereby they could advance to that man his unemployment insurance payments and collect them from the unemployment insurance office when they come due? Instead of having a man wait two or three weeks for his unemployment insurance he could get it from the welfare officers. They will co-operate. They do co-operate with the workmen's compensation.
A man in my riding who has a claim against the workmen's compensation does not have to wait until he can draw his compensation from the board. He can go to the welfare officers. They are provided with a form by the workmen's compensation board through which the man can immediately begin drawing his workmen's compensation. If, after the case has been carefully examined it is found that he has no claim on workmen's compensation, then the township has to stand the loss, and welfare officers tell me that they are prepared to do that. They cannot sit there and see people starve for lack of a few dollars.
But in very few cases has it occurred where they have not been compensated by the workmen's compensation board. So far as the welfare board in my particular riding is concerned, I can assure the minister that they will co-operate fully with him in overcoming that difficulty of having unemployed people wait even nine days or five days. If it could be settled in five days, it would be easy. But even that will imply twelve days, if it is reduced to five.
The point I suggest the minister must understand is that in most cases the working man has no income, once his pay cheque stops. He has no reserve. He cannot afford to wait ten days, fifteen days, or two or three weeks before he gets his unemployment insurance. In many cases his pay cheque is spent before he gets it. When he gets out

The Address-Mr. Wright of employment, and has to wait, he has no recourse but to run bills with his neighbouring grocer and butcher.
There are one or two other points I should like to mention-and in doing so I shall be as brief as possible. I think something should be done to ensure that those who pay unemployment insurance over a period of years are not rendered ineligible by reason of some technicality. I know the department has taken almost every precaution it can. However, there have come to my attention several cases of men who paid unemployment insurance for two or three years and then became employers again. I have in mind the case of a building contractor who went back to work, paying unemployment insurance for a while, only to find that he had not enough stamps to entitle him to unemployment insurance. I have taken those cases to the officer in charge. I will say this for the officers, that in every case they have taken the trouble to make investigations. In some cases they have found there were technical errors and, as a result, the unemployment insurance has been paid.
But what happens? Those offices are so overcrowded, they are so bogged down with from 800 to 1,100 people coming in every day for unemployment insurance, that the ordinary individual just does not have a chance in the world to have his case taken up by the supervisor, or anyone other than a man or woman at the desk. The cases have to be rushed through, without the opportunity for proper investigation.
I have only one more suggestion in this connection: Unemployment supervisors-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not expect it would be necessary for me to take part in the debate at this point. However, as it would seem that Your Honour was about to put the question, I believe I should say a few words with regard to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) and the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce).
If hon. members could see my notes, and how closely they follow the speech made by


the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), I am sure they would be surprised. Perhaps, however, it is not so surprising when it is realized that we both represent farming constituencies in western Canada, and that both of us have farmed and therefore know some of the problems connected with agriculture.
I am not going to quote again many of the quotations placed on record by the hon. member for Acadia, when he was referring to what had been said by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and by Mr. Han-nam, the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. But I do intend to emphasize some of the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Acadia. I do so because I believe they are important, and that they represent the thinking of a great portion of the agricultural industry at this time.
I was in Europe for a short time this winter, and I can assure the house that on coming back to Canada I appreciate more than ever our position and our ability to meet our needs in this country, and to produce surpluses of many products needed not only in Europe but in many other parts of the world.
Yet we find in Canada, as has been indicated, an agricultural policy with respect to the production of food which indicates that we must keep our production of food in Canada in balance with the amount that we can hope to sell on our home market, and that we must ignore the need for food we see throughout the world today.
This is not new. This policy has been the same for five years. About that time Sir John Boyd Orr, then head of the food and agriculture organization, made the statement that three out of four people in the world went to bed hungry every night of the year. I have never seen that statement denied by any authority, and I take it therefore that it is a true statement of the position in the world today with regard to food.
Yet we in Canada seem unable to devise t financial policy which will enable us to distribute some of the production that we could have if we were to use our full productive capacity in this country. I think some of the suggestions made by the hon. member for Acadia are good ones. As a matter of fact they are suggestions this group made back in 1946 and 1947. Our leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), stated at that time that Canada should be prepared to export some of our products, and accept in payment for (them sterling or other currencies. If it was impossible for those countries requiring food to obtain the necessary dollars, he said we

might give consideration to accepting their own currency. If we accepted that currency we could use it in assisting these countries in developing some of their own resources.
As I say, we advocated that back in 1946 and 1947. But the government has never seen fit to accept that policy. We have heard a lot of pious wishes; we hear speeches made by different members of the government indicating the need, and indicating that to stop communism in the world it will be necessary for us to feed some of the hungry peoples of the world. But there has been very little action, very little by way of practical action to implement that policy.
I agree fully with the hon. member for Acadia when he says it is possible to do that. And unless we do something about that situation, so long as the people of the rest of the world see in Canada the possibilities of greater food production and, at the same time, see our Minister of Agriculture and the heads of our farm organizations saying that at least we must contain production to the point where we can sell it at a reasonable price to our own people, at a time when the peoples in other countries are hungry, we are just asking for the spread of communism in the world today. Make no mistake about that. We are giving those people the type of ammunition they need and which no army can stop, no matter how much we spend on armed forces throughout the world today. Unless we are prepared to do more than that, then I say that a great deal of the money we are spending on preparedness and in building up protective forces will be wasted. I think that point should be emphasized.
Then a word with regard to our home market. Is there room for more production to supply our home market? Mention has been made of the fact that the war veterans allowance does not provide sufficient purchasing power to those receiving it to maintain a decent standard of living. The $40 old age pension does not provide sufficient purchasing power for many of our older people to maintain the standard of living that should be possible in this country. No pensions are provided for the incapacitated and those suffering from permanent disability. Many other classes could be named, such as retired civil servants and people living on fixed incomes or annuities which they purchased back in the 1930's or early 1940's when the dollar was worth much more than it is worth today. These people are finding that when their annuities come due they will not purchase what is required to give them a decent standard of living. All these people could consume more in the way of food than they are at the present time.
The Address-Mr. Wright
Then as to the consumption of milk, back in 1946 and 1947 when we subsidized the sale of milk, when milk could be obtained for ten or twelve cents a quart, our consumption was much larger than it is today. Because of the reduced ability of those who need milk for their children to buy it we find that the consumption of milk and other dairy products is being reduced. We cannot get a greater production of milk unless the producer is paid an incentive price to produce.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has stated time and again that in setting floor prices under agricultural products they were not considered1 to be incentive prices, that it was not the policy of the government to set floor prices under agricultural products on an incentive basis, but simply to prevent a debacle as far as the sale of that particular product was concerned.
Unless the farmer receives an incentive price he is not going to produce to capacity, either for the home market or for the world market. Surely we have enough intelligence in Canada today to devise ways and means of giving incentive prices to the producers of our food products. When the gold mines found that their costs of production were such that they could not get a fair return, they were able to come to the government and get a subsidy in the form of an incentive price for their production. Which is the more important in the world today, the production of gold or the production of food? Which is the most likely to stop the spread of communism throughout the world? In my opinion to ask the question is almost ridiculous. You cannot eat gold, you cannot wear it, you cannot do anything with it except bury it in another hole in the ground.
These are matters which are important and which come directly under the amendment moved by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair). Therefore it is the intention of this group to support that amendment. We believe that we should have maximum production in this country. How can we get greater production? I want to speak for a moment or two about the Carrot river section which covers my own constituency and northwestern Manitoba. The northeastern part of that valley contains the largest new area of productive land available in Canada today. This section stretches up through the Carrot river valley, through the estuary of the Carrot river and the Saskatchewan river into lake Winnipeg.
It is estimated that in this area there are from 2,500,000 to 3,000,000 acres of the most productive land to be found anywhere in Canada. All this is available for development provided certain diking is done and

The Address-Mr. Wright certain flood control measures are carried out. During the last year P.F.R.A. engineers have been making surveys. I have not as yet seen their report, but people in that area on whose judgment I rely tell me that there is no doubt that this land can be made available for an expenditure of around $5 per acre. That is probably more than the provincial governments of Manitoba and Saskatchewan could afford to spend, but it is not more than the Dominion of Canada can afford to spend.
By developing that area we can put into cultivation one of the most productive sections in western Canada. This section would produce wheat, not at the average yield of some 16 bushels per acre which has prevailed throughout western Canada, but at the rate of 25 bushels to the acre, which is the rate which has been maintained here for the last 25 years. Not only can wheat be raised in this area; coarse grains can be produced and the largest production of sweet clover and alfalfa seed in Canada is in that area today. Mixed farming could be carried on. There could be an abundant production to be used to feed some of the people I have mentioned, both at home and abroad.
In my opinion there is no area in Canada today where such returns can be obtained for the expenditure of a similar amount of money, and this would include oil, minerals or other developments. I believe that this government should provide the necessary funds to carry this development into effect in the next two or three years.
I should like to refer for a moment to the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) and which refers to the serious situation existing today in the following words:
(c) To establish a federal authority to deal with meat and with dairy products during the present emergency, with power to establish floor prices for producers, to protect consumers by control of retail prices, and to arrange for the equitable distribution of such products during the said emergency.
While we are urging that these measures should be taken now to take care of the present emergency, we submit that similar measures should have been put into effect some time ago. As a matter of fact, last summer when a disastrous drop in the price of hogs on our Canadian markets occurred we asked that an investigation should be made by the combines commissioner. I have in my hand a letter which I passed across the floor of the house to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) on November 15 of last year. I am going to read it to the house to indicate what

I was asking for at that time. It is addressed to the Hon. Stuart Garson, Minister of Justice, and reads as follows:
Dear Sir:
May I, in accordance with section 10A of the Combines Investigation Act, chapter 26, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, register the following complaint and request an investigation thereof by the commissioner of the Combines Investigation Act. Between July 21 of this year and September 22, prices for grade A hogs dropped from $40 per hundredweight to $29 per hundredweight on the Toronto market. (See table I). A similar drop took place in every other major centre in Canada. In other words, there was a decrease in hog prices in this period of approximately 25 per cent.
The reason for this drop is not readily apparent. As you will note from weekly figures on total inspected slaughterings (table I) and from the comparative figures for the previous three years, there was not during these three months any abnormal increase in hog marketings which might account for the depression in price. The domestic disappearance of pork from inspected slaughterings was 655,176,000 in the year ending October 1, 1951, compared with 629,573,000 the year before. It is evident, therefore, that there has been no substantial drop in demand for pork products.
May I also draw your attention to the fact that during the period under discussion there was no similar drop in the retail prices of pork products to the consumer (see table III). Between July and October there was a slight drop, approximately 10 per cent, in the retail price of ham, Montreal, and of pork shoulder. The price of pork loins remained about the same while the price of side bacon rose a little. In any event there has been no general decrease in retail pork prices of the magnitude of 25 per cent. Such decrease as there has been has lagged far behind the drop in the price of hogs both in time and in amount.
It may be suggested that there is inevitably a considerable delay between the time a change takes place in the price of hogs and the time that change in price is reflected on the retail market, the delay being occasioned by the length of time required for processing and distribution.
I want hon. members to mark this.
But may I call your attention to the fact that when meat prices, beef and pork, rose sharply following decontrol of prices late in 1947 and the negotiation of new British contracts early in 1948, there was no such delay in passing the increases on to the consumer. The following statement was made with respect to this matter by the royal commission on prices, 1948, at page 100 of volume III of their report:
"Those firms owning beef and pork in cold storage at the end of 1947 made substantial fortuitous gains as a result of inventory appreciation, as market prices advanced with the increased United Kingdom contract prices . . . The four firms, Canada Packers, Swift Canadian, Burns and Wilsil, held over two-thirds of the total cold storage stocks. The inventories of beef as of January 1, 1948, were at record levels: those of pork, while not a record, were relatively large."
The royal commission noted the three largest packing firms in Canada made a combined net profit of $4-3 million in the four months following the removal of price controls, compared with less than $1 million in the corresponding period the year before, and that a substantial portion of this increase was inventory profit.
May I, therefore, request that the commissioner investigate and report on:

(1)	the reasons for the 25 per cent decrease in hog prices between mid-July and the end of September of this year;
(2)	whether there was any agreement or arrangement, actual or tacit, among the major packing companies or any of them in respect of this decrease in hog prices;
(3)	the reasons why the decrease in the price of pork to the producers was not passed on to the consumer promptly and in like proportion;
(4)	whether there was any agreement or arrangement, actual or tacit, among the major packing companies or any of them in respect of the failure to decrease retail prices as indicated;
(5)	whether there is any agreement or arrangement, actual or tacit, among the major packing companies or any of them in maintaining wholesale meat prices to the retail trade in Canada as a whole or in any part thereof.
I received a reply to that letter on February 23, or three months and a week after I had written my letter. I received it just a week before the present session commenced. I am going to read part of what the commissioner stated and ask the permission of the house to have the whole letter placed on the record. The last part of the letter reads as follows:
In case you wish to bring this letter and the material attached to the attention of others I am enclosing several copies.
In other words, he wishes his reply to be given publicity. I want to comment on certain paragraphs in his letter. So that no one will think that I am doing so unfairly or taking anything out of its context, I would ask the permission of the house to have the letter printed in full so that all members will have an equal opportunity of seeing what is in it and so that it will be given the publicity for which the commissioner asks.

No, I am not going to read it. Permission has been refused by one member. He is perfectly justified in doing so if he feels that way about it, and I cannot have it included unless he is prepared to withdraw his objection. I certainly do not intend to read the letter. However, the letter shows quite clearly, and the commissioner goes to great lengths to prove, that the prices charged to the consumer for these pork products did drop; and that while that drop was delayed the benefit of the reduced prices to the producer eventually did reach the consumer. But at no point in the letter does the commissioner try to prove that those reductions were in the same ratio as the increases in the prices to the consumer when prices to the producer had increased. I hope no one will think my criticism is unfair because he cannot read the letter itself. If he wishes to do so he will find a copy in my office that he can read at any time. I say that nowhere in that letter does the commissioner try to prove that the drop in prices to the consumer

That is the meat of the matter. It is aE very well to say that the infallible rule of supply and demand controls prices. Eventually prices do increase as the demand increases and drop as the demand decreases; but the middleman in this country is able to hold back those advantages which should1 come to the consumer with a drop in the price to the producer, and is able to pass on quickly any increase in the price paid the producer; and it is by reason of this lag that profits are made in this country. Make no mistake about it; profits are being made, as was demonstrated before the price spreads committee when controls were taken off back in 1946. At that time it was demonstrated, as I have indicated in the letter that was sent to the commissioner, that a fortuitous gain of over $3 million was made by the packing plants of this country, by increasing the prices on meat they already had in storage, which they had bought from the farmers at the prices which obtained before the controls were lifted. The same condition applied last summer with regard to pork. Why did the price of pork drop in July? That happened because the bureau of statistics issued1 -a statement showing the number of sows that had been bred and the amount of pork that would probably come on the market in the fall. Did they wait until the pork came on the market? Oh, no; prices dropped right away, within a week after those figures were made public. But when the bureau of statistics issues statistics indicating that there is going to be a scarcity, do you think the market reacts immediately? Oh, no; it waits until the scarcity actuaEy occurs before it reacts.
These are things that should be looked into under the Combines Investigation Act, to determine whether the consumers and producers are being treated fairly by the people who distribute meat products in this country. Until the commissioner is prepared to act promptly in these matters he can expect criticism to continue in respect to what the producer receives for his product and what the consumer finally has to pay for it. These facts are well known and have been brought to the attention of the government and the combines investigation commissioner many times. Until these things; are investigated; until I have more evidence than is contained in the letter I wished to have appear in Hansard-and I am sure the hon. member who objected did no service to this house-I am not satisfied with the situation that exists today.

There is an emergency situation in this country because of the foot-and-mouth disease. Again we are going to see these violent fluctuations. One part of Canada wEl be paying more than it can afford for meat, while another part -where there is a surplus will have reduced prices. In the meantime those who control the speed with which price changes are reflected in lower prices to the consumer or higher prices to the producer will again reap a harvest unless the government is prepared to appoint a board or a controller to see that there is fair play; and surely in such an emergency the government should be prepared to act. That is all the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) is asking. He wants fair play to both the producer and the consumer, through the appointment of a board with power to see that somebody does not reap an unfair profit out of the disaster that has struck our livestock industry. It is a disaster. I think I am conservative when I say that the price of every beef and dairy animal in Canada has been reduced by at least $50 in the last month because of the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease. Who is going to reap the benefit of that? Certainly it is not the producer, and as far as prices are concerned it is not going to be the consumer unless this government has the courage to see that there is fair play in this matter.
I want to urge the necessity of appointing a board or controller at this time to see that justice is done, so that someone does not reap a completely unearned profit as a result of the disaster the foot-and-mouth disease has caused to our livestock industry. I am sure that is the wish of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I am sure it is the wish of the consumers of this country, and it should be the wish of every member of this house. I hope members on both the government and opposition sides will support this measure.
